I complain a lot about the state of fighting games as a whole, how certain franchises refuse to move past the golden days of their arcade ports and how others seemingly get abandoned through a lack of support of their publishers and/or developers - but then there's Tekken  The game that I never quite got on well, even back on the PS2 when I first booted up the demo for Tekken 4 and found the clunky 2.5D fighter style to not work well with my brawler and Soul Edge infused brain.  But, it's legitimately been 20 years since then, and somehow I've found myself enamoured by this game, anyway. While I think that, visually, I prefer the predecessors less busy overall aesthetic, I can't lie and say that Tekken 8 is ugly.  From a gameplay perspective, I also think that it does a much better job of allowing people of all skill levels to find enjoyment in this one than most of it's contemporaries - while I'm a bit iffy on how the "casual" control scheme works, I understand it's purpose and I think that the compromise of easier moment to moment gameplay with a damage penalty is an interesting thing to have.  Audio wise, I find some of the samples used in the new tracks to be grating to my ears. I miss some of the original Tekken 4 and 5 tracks, and I will always miss the angsty teeny deep voice announcer of 5. Other than that, this game is punchy in all the right ways. Haha.  Tekken 8 is not only an accessible entry in a genre that's ultra-elitist and alienating to people who have not played fighting games before, but it's also one of the better ones - which is funny, considering Tekken fans will have you think Namco shot their dogs and killed their families.  If I had to give it a rating out of 10 as a fighting game, [b]I'd give it an 8/10.[/b] If I had to give it a rating out of 10 as a videogame on it's own, [b]I'd give it a 6/10[/b] (I'm a casual fighting game fan)

[h2]QUICK VERDICT[/h2]  Tekken 8 is a powerful step forward for one of fighting games’ most important series. It respects Tekken’s legacy while giving it a faster, more aggressive, and welcoming identity. Heat, recoverable health, excellent training tools, strong offline content, and improved online play make it immediately exciting while retaining enough depth to last for years.  [h2]PROS & CONS[/h2]  [h3]Pros[/h3]  * Excellent fighting system * Strong single-player content * Brilliant training and replay tools * Improved online play * Incredible visuals and sound  [h3]Cons[/h3]  * Offensive pressure can feel overwhelming * Some characters receive little story attention * Special Style is limited long term * A few uneven cutscene transitions  [h2]STORY[/h2]  The Dark Awakens continues the conflict between Jin Kazama and Kazuya Mishima. It explores power, family trauma, hatred, and Jin’s attempt to escape the damage passed down through the Mishima bloodline.  The campaign fully embraces Tekken’s dramatic identity. There are huge anime-style battles, emotional speeches, impossible odds, and plenty of ridiculous moments. It is not subtle, but Tekken works best when it confidently embraces its own chaos.  The story lasts around three to four hours and combines cinematic scenes with playable fights. Several familiar characters appear, although some are far more important than others.  Newcomers should still be able to follow the central conflict, and the Gallery includes summaries of previous games.  [h2]GAMEPLAY[/h2]  Tekken 8’s combat is where it truly shines. Movement, spacing, punishment, sidestepping, blocking, and reading your opponent remain essential. It does not abandon the foundations of Tekken but builds new systems around them.  The biggest addition is Heat. Every round begins with Heat available, giving characters stronger offensive options, chip damage, enhanced moves, and powerful follow-up attacks. It encourages players to move forward, take risks, and build momentum.  This works alongside recoverable health. Some damage becomes grey health that can be recovered by attacking. You cannot simply wait behind your guard. You have to fight for it, giving every round a constant sense of urgency.  Tekken 8 still rewards patience and defence, but it pushes players to act more frequently. You must decide when to activate Heat, continue pressure, recover health, or save an important option.  The result is fast and exciting, although the increased aggression can become overwhelming. Pressure-heavy characters can feel terrifying once Heat is active, and blocking while taking chip damage can be stressful.  Tekken 8 also has some of the best learning tools in the genre. Training mode includes combo challenges, punishment training, detailed attack information, pinned moves, and save states.  The replay system is even better. You can watch a match, pause during a difficult moment, take control, and test possible answers. It turns mistakes into practical learning opportunities.  Special Style gives beginners access to useful moves through simple button presses. It is not a replacement for properly learning a character, but it is helpful when starting out.  [h2]CONTENT[/h2]  Arcade Quest is a clever introduction to the game. Your avatar visits arcade locations, battles opponents, and gradually learns important mechanics. It captures the feeling of joining a fighting game community, losing, improving, and finding your place.  The Tekken Fight Lounge gives online play a similar social atmosphere. It is not essential, but it gives the game more personality than a basic selection of menus.  Solo players also have plenty to enjoy through character episodes, Arcade Quest, Super Ghost Battle, training modes, and the main story.  Super Ghost Battle lets you fight CPU opponents based on real player habits. You can download ghosts from other players or fight your own ghost to identify bad habits. It cannot replace real competition, but it is a great practice tool.  [h2]VISUALS & SOUND[/h2]  Tekken 8 looks incredible. Character models are detailed, animations feel powerful, and every attack has a satisfying sense of weight. Sparks, lighting, slow motion, camera movement, and environmental destruction make each battle feel intense.  The new characters also stand out immediately. Victor’s flashy spy-inspired style, Azucena’s energetic personality, and Reina’s aggressive Mishima techniques all feel distinct.  The only noticeable issue is the transition between real-time gameplay and certain pre-rendered scenes, where lighting and colour grading can occasionally look inconsistent.  The soundtrack matches the game’s aggressive style, while heavy sound effects make attacks and Heat activation feel satisfying.  The Jukebox is one of the best additions for longtime fans. It allows stage music to be replaced with tracks from across Tekken’s history, making the soundtrack a celebration of the entire series.  [h2]PERFORMANCE & ONLINE[/h2]  Tekken 8 feels smooth, responsive, and visually stable.  The online experience is a major improvement over Tekken 7. Cross-play keeps the community connected, matches generally feel reliable, and rematches load much faster.  Poor connections can still cause issues, but the overall experience is strong. The faster rematch system keeps sets moving and removes much of the unnecessary waiting found in the previous game.  [h2]DIFFICULTY[/h2]  [h3]7 / 10[/h3]  Tekken 8 is still difficult. Huge move lists, movement techniques, matchup knowledge, and long-term character mastery require patience.  However, this is also the most approachable Tekken has ever been. Arcade Quest introduces mechanics gradually, training mode provides detailed tools, replays explain mistakes, and Special Style lets beginners start fighting before memorising complicated inputs.  The game remains demanding, but it gives players practical ways to understand what went wrong and improve.  [h2]RECOMMENDED FOR[/h2]  [h3]Recommended for:[/h3]  * Tekken and fighting game fans * Players who enjoy deep combat * Beginners wanting strong learning tools * Fans of stylish Japanese action * Solo and online players  [h3]Not recommended for:[/h3]  * Players who strongly dislike difficult games * Anyone wanting an extremely simple fighter * Players frustrated by pressure-heavy combat * Anyone unwilling to practise  [h2]PERSONAL EXPERIENCE[/h2]  What I respect most about Tekken 8 is how confidently it moves forward. It does not feel like a safe sequel, but it also does not disrespect the past.  Heat pushed me to attack, recover health, take space, and stop waiting for perfect opportunities. The training tools made improvement feel achievable, the story gave the experience heart, and the Jukebox reminded me how much history this series carries.  [h2]FINAL VERDICT[/h2]  Tekken 8 is an excellent fighting game and one of the strongest entries in the series. It retains the movement, punishment, depth, character identity, and legacy that made Tekken special while making matches faster and more aggressive.  Heat and recoverable health create a powerful new rhythm. The training features make learning easier, the offline modes give solo players plenty to enjoy, and the online experience is a clear improvement over Tekken 7.  Even with a few small issues, Tekken 8 feels confident and built to last.  It honours the past, but it keeps walking forward.  Read my complete Tekken 8 review here: https://hermittalksgames.com/reviews/tekken-8-review

Tekken 8 is an incredibly fun and explosive fighting game that is mired in controversy resulting from a terrible mishandling of its post-launch period across the board as well as gross negligence and miscommunication between the developers and the most vocal part of its fanbase. It's hard to say who is really at fault here, but it's obvious that there is a massive disconnect between the publisher, development studio, and core audience which has resulted in an undeniably turbulent post-launch period that has done catastrophic damage to the brand's image and lead to the exit of several high profile individuals from within Bandai Namco.  It's important to acknowledge the controversy surrounding this game because I think that this has ultimately gotten in the way of Tekken 8's image as a fighting game; and, personally speaking, despite all of the negativity that seems to surround it, Tekken 8 is the most fun I've had in any of the current major fighting games on the market that are still being actively supported. I come from a predominantly Street Fighter-dominated background, but I say with no hyperbole or exaggeration that I enjoy Tekken more this time around. That may be going against the popular narrative; but, Tekken 8, despite its problems, gives me the type of experience that I'm looking for when nearly every other current fighter inevitably disappoints or disillusions me for one reason or another. Once you cut through all the noise, the core of Tekken 8 is still very strong.  That isn't to say that the game doesn't have problems. Balancing has been a big issue and the game is also extremely volatile, resulting in massively lopsided rounds from one to the next. But this is a trend that is not exclusive to the current iteration of Tekken and is seen in nearly every other modern fighter, which all prioritize a gameplay loop focused on relentless aggression, weak defensive play, and giving players free resources from the start of every round. This is a pretty big antithesis to how fighters have usually been up to this point, where resources were something you had to earn over the course of a match and players with superior defense would usually reign supreme. If we look back to Tekken 7 and Street Fighter IV, we see that those games were aggressively defensive. The current trend of fighters being the opposite of that feels like a natural by-product of the pendulum simply swinging the other way. Given enough time we may eventually see fighters move back towards more deliberate and careful play, though I personally hope we never go back to the extreme turtleness of the two aforementioned titles.  Anyway, the point of this review is that I simply want to say that despite Tekken 8's issues, I still think it offers the most fun to be had out of any modern fighter currently available—at least, its specific brand of chaos in the current era is the one that I enjoy the most. Mechanically, the game is much more aligned with what I'm looking for in a fighting game than its contemporaries. The problem is that Tekken 8 is also vastly different from what the most vocal part of the Tekken community claims to want. Personally, I never really clicked with Tekken 6 or 7, opting to play other games instead during those times. I don't have much experience with the series other than Tekken 5 Dark Resurrection, which I enjoyed, so I am essentially a newcomer. For me, Tekken 8 offers what I want: fast, explosive, and exciting gameplay backed up by gorgeous visuals and a mostly killer soundtrack (which is a huge improvement over Tekken 7, by the way, with most of the ear-grating wubwub being snuffed out).  There's no doubt that there's a lot of stuff regarding Tekken 8's gameplay that's problematic, but I don't agree with the consensus that the HEAT system is to blame. HEAT is an incredibly fun mechanic, but its been shoved into a game that also has oppressively small stages replete with hazards that allow for free combo extensions that when combined with the HEAT system result in cutscene length combos that are a big source of ire for most of the player base. I don't want a Tekken game where characters can do less things; I love that Tekken 8 has made nearly everyone in the roster ridiculously powerful in their own right, but the rest of the game needs to be designed accordingly around that. I think Tekken 8's core gameplay would be in a much better place if the stages were adjusted to compensate. This means no longer giving the corner for free to the player who lands the first big hit, and to reduce or eliminate stage hazards across the board, making them much more difficult to achieve than they are currently. As the game stands, it's simply much too easy to bulldoze your opponent when every stage is a walk-in closet with explosives strapped to every corner. The stage hazards are by far my least favourite aspect of Tekken 8 and I'd like to see them toned down to allow for a greater focus on meaningful interactions between players. HEAT by itself is much less problematic on the game's more open stages like Yakushima and Baobab Horizon when its use doesn't automatically trap the opponent against the wall in a 50/50 blender because every stage is so oppressively small.  Despite its volatility and serious issues with overall game balance, Tekken 8 is still an incredibly fun game and it looks incredible in motion. Unfortunately, it is plagued with a lot of other problems unrelated to its gameplay, such as the fact that almost all of its DLC is recycled from the last game or has been incredibly tone deaf and not want people wanted. Brand new characters that were DLC in Tekken 7 have no business being DLC [i]again[/i] and should have been included in the base roster. The battle passes are an absolute joke, with 90% of what's included being utterly meaningless content. The customization system—awesome as a general concept—is very lazy and lacks the depth of previous games in the series and other titles by the same publisher. The game's modes still don't include very good tools for learning learn how to play and much learning and research outside of the game itself will be required. Tekken characters have expansive movelists that feature hundreds of moves; as a new player, it's impossible to know which moves to prioritize and this can only be learned through sheer hours of raw gameplay experience. This also means that Tekken is, by its very nature, extremely knowledge-check heavy and it forces new players to go through a ruthless initiation period. It also has a serious smurfing problem—the quick match queue is essentially shark infested waters, so its recommended that all players queue into ranked. Arcade mode is marginally improved over Tekken 7 but is still very underwhelming. It is far too easy and has no story to speak of. Arcade and Character Episodes really should have been consolidated into one mode rather than being separate. There's just no reason for these modes to exist simultaneously as separate entities.  Tekken 8 is the story of a good core game that has been terribly mismanaged by a huge disconnect between the publisher, developers, and fan base. This rift has resulted in a game that no longer feels like it has a clear vision of what it's trying to accomplish. But, when it's all said and done, is Tekken 8 still fun to play? Yeah, It is. I've been having a blast with it. It's incredibly fun and has been my most played game on Steam for two years in a row now; it's currently on track for a third. I'd advise people to give it a chance—check it out on sale and just accept that every fighting game has its own brand of dumb that you either deal with because the game is fun and you like the characters, or you don't and you move on to something else. In my case, Tekken 8's brand of dumb is exactly what I want and is much more entertaining than what's being offered by its contemporaries. See you out on the battlefield. Tekken 8 is an amazing fighting game. It looks good, it plays good. Yes, Bandai messed up big time. Not once, not even twice, they in fact managed to fail for two entire seasons and still couldn't figure out the identitiy of the core gameplay. While trying to make defensive gameplay more valuable, they inadvertently made offensive gameplay the only way to play.  Everytime they try to nerf or buff certain moves or specific characters, they tend to not change the char or move itself but rather the game system itself and how its supposed to work when stuff happens - that is almost every single time a huge step back because it messes with other chars that were not intented to be changed.   Yet, its fun if you don't try to be the absolute best of the best. Messy stuff happens, there is a lot of timing and luck involved but if you stay consistent, you just might win more than you lose. Ever since i stopped caring as much for the little things and started to simply accept that i just was not good enough, trying again, adapt to rude playstyles, things got better.  Of Course the community tends to be toxic, especially with the characters that they do not like to play against - no matter what you play, someone always will say that you a noob for playing this.  While i agree on designing a couple characters that are MEANT TO BE EASIER, they have to have clear weaknesses and most of the roaster DOES HAVE THOSE WEAKNESSES that you can use to your advantage. Of course though, there will be plenty situations in which you just feel robbed too.  My absolute favourite word in this game (and honestly its applyable for quite literally anything in life) is PATIENCE. Patience is a virtue, it has more value than most think. No matter if your opponent has flashy strings and animations or simply tries to pressure you with insane 50/50 mixups, patience almost always pays out positively for you.  The Battlepasses since they got released for the first time, they all, i promise, ALL OF THEM, simply sucked. I don't see value in them since most of the stuff does not even look like theres been any work done for those cosmetics. Yes, the same ball now with a different colour thats supposed to float above your head does not make it worth it. The profile banners are useless. The loading screens can be nice but i just wish for additional rage art animations.  I like the Lounge though, thats a nice thing that makes you feel like a part of a community.  Yes the balancing is crap for the most part but it seriously is not as unplayable as many people try to claim. Sometimes you lose because you bad, sometimes you lose because of bad luck, sometimes people use scummy strategies with frame traps that are difficult to get out of but theres just as many rounds that you absolutely stomp and you really FEEL the TEKKEN in this game.  It is worth it. I promise.

alright, i've gotten to the 1000 point so i think its fair i get to make a review  Tekken 8 is a fun game. This is coming from someone who plays it casually  this game is genuinely fun. i understand that in the games life span that its had its ups and downs, which happens to most games in this industry. Tekken had a rocky launch and a horrible, HORRIBLE season 2. Season 3 has been the most fun i've had with the game since release despite combos now being shorter (which is a VERY VERY good thing, i just like my combos) and certain moves on characters not being changed or being changed drastically (looking at you Jin heat smash). Tbh people like to give this game ♥♥♥♥ for no reason. most people who actually love tekken will play it regardless and you can genuinely have a great time playing whether its ranked or just against your buddies.   hell i'll even say this: since i've played tekken and mained Kazuya, i have drastically improved in other games due to how you have to think and function in tekken. learning spacing, when to use certain moves, plus and minus frames,  whiff punishing, even outside of fighting games with games like Quaver or FNF or Rhythm Haven, hell even the new lego batman game which plays like the arkham games (which is peak go play ts RN) im hitting crit hits with ease and building meter like crazy. Tekken has helped me learn how to play other games more effectively by being a difficult game. being a 3d fighter instead of 2d meaning you dont just have to sit there and block until your opponent throws something hell unsafe or getting put into a corner and watching as time ticks down.   the bad part about tekken is just the people who dont know who you fight against. there are still lots of cheaters who are buns and people who do toxic stuff in ranked queue or player matches. tbh theres no escaping that in any game and you kinda have to live with it here. theres also character balance, everyone is just busted besides like 2-3 characters who actually take hella skill to utilize to the fullest (Bryan, Kaz, DVJ) but that also kinda adds a bit of charm to the game. anyone can use any character and be good with them, you just gotta practice  TLDR - if you like the series, the memes, the characters, the combos, the 3d aspect then the game is peak. if you dont wanna do all the studying of frames and learning punishes and trying to do precise combos then  dont play ranked and just fight your buddies, or just dont buy the game.   7.8/10, will still play it regardless of how broken it can get

Yes, there are plenty of options for both offline and online play.  Even so, Tekken 8 disappoints.  The feel of the game simply isn't there.  The rhythm and flow of the fighting have gotten worse over the last few generations, and this is the worst of the bunch.  The addition of "modern" features don't fit the old Tekken combat system well at all, and as a result, the fighting itself feels like a jumbled mess.  The Story mode is all over the place, the arcade mode is straight garbage, and the arcade combat mode (different thing here) is both unimpressive and surprisingly easy - even on the hardest difficulty.  The game's menus are a joke, and it's constantly screaming at you to buy the latest DLC.  It's more difficult to set up proper custom tournaments than it should be, the netcode is still sloppy, and the lobbies are a mess.    They're still trying to do "something" with the character customization, but that's been pretty much garbage since Tekken 5.  They really should have stuck with the old-school "Win with a character, unlock another outfit for that character" routine, at the very least.   Tekken 8 feels like it's trying to do too much, and it can't decide what kind of fighting game it really wants to be.  As such, it's not really good at any of it.  Looks nice, though.

Do you enjoy getting hit once and then having a cutscene for the rest of the match, or playing against a character who was just buffed so much that they could kill God? Well, this is the game for you, you masochists. As of writing this, I have been beaten by a Jack-8 who used a throw and one other move the entire match, a King who spammed grabs, and a bunch of players who pressed the button that plays the game for you. I first played Tekken 7 at a friend's house and fell in love with it, and I waited 5 years to finally get a gaming computer that could run it. When they announced Tekken 8, I was so excited to play it even though it was around $120 at launch. I didn't have a computer that could run it, so I waited a year and a half, and I got one a few months before Christmas. When I saw that it was on sale for $65, I bought it and started playing. I sucked, but I was so determined to master the game. I watched tutorials and I practiced, and when I finally played multiplayer, I got my ass whooped. AT THAT POINT I REALIZED THAT YOU HAVE TO KNOW EVERY CHARACTER'S MOVES TO WIN. IF YOU DON'T, YOU'LL JUST LOSE AND LOSE AND LOSE. I will admit that I suck, but if you do want to play this casually, you won't get too far in ranked. But if you're willing and you have the time, you can get pretty far. My opinion will probably change later on, but right now I'm just pissed. It's not a horrible game. I really enjoy playing against my friend. He's really good and beats me all the time, but it's fun playing with him.  IF YOU DON'T WANNA READ ALL THAT, THIS IS THE MOST HONEST OPINION I CAN GIVE: the characters are really unbalanced, the game is just about who can hit first, and if you don't, you'll be thrown around the stage like a baby fighting Conor McGregor. Every update, there are a bunch of moves added that have not been tested. The most broken character I can think of is Jack-8. If you do get this game, don't expect it to be easy. It's the hardest fighting game I have ever played. Oh yeah, the DLCs are ridiculously expensive. Wanna play Heihachi? Yeah, that's gonna be 20 bucks buddy. It really makes you feel like they are trying to squeeze every last penny out of you if you want to play a locked character and the cherry on top is that they wont ever listen to the community.

There is some salt in this review, so take that into account. I do, however, speak not from my heart, but from my mind. I have over 3k hours into this game, drive two hours to make locals every few weeks, and spent a lot of time on this game as my main hobby. No more.   I regret investing time into this game. The game is three years old and it still doesn't know what it's trying to be. Character tuning and nerfs make little rhyme or reason. If you buy a DLC character, be especially wary. They will let your character be too strong and then nerf it into the ground the next season after most of the purchases/interest for said character are over. This fosters animus between players of this character and the rest of the community. When the aforementioned next season occurs and your DLC character gets nerfed into the ground--not always immediately at the start of the season--no one will care because your character was a nightmare the season prior.   I also don't think this game knows what it wants to be. It fluctuates between trying to be a super fast paced exciting game and an old school Tekken game. Nostalgia and frustration do blur some lines, but it feels like T8 doesn't hit either target audience.   I'm tired of grinding a game, watching videos, following the esports, making lobbies, labbing, and doing the things I'm supposed to do just to run into an overly tuned character that won't get touched because it's too profitable. AK is still an overly tuned monster of a character. King, ironically, not a DLC, but has such a huge following that he has to be kept OP.   The game hasn't taken modernity into account, either. Given the lay of the land, it's easier now than ever to KBD (trivialized, sadly)  do electrics, wave-dash, etc. You would think some of those abilities would be tempered since they are easier to do, but no.    There are other QoL issues, too. Too many mids look like lows and too many lows look like mids. The combo system is an incoherent mess, the infamous 'T8 camera man' behaves like he's drunk. Moves that have no business crushing or evading do, hit boxes are random, etc. Characters seem to either have no moves that you can reliably step and walk OR everything can be stepped and walked.   This isn't a well made game. If I could go back in time, I would never have poured my heart and soul into this title. Lord knows they nickel and dime the players who want to support the product and have cool customs, too. Basic eye colors are locked behind battle passes? We waited years for....black lipstick?

Alright, lemme be honest. Tekken 8 is a fun game. Playing with friends and family? Great time. But once you start climbing the online ranks, things get a bit more complicated. Compared to Tekken 7, some mechanics have been simplified (the assist mode is the clearest example) The game is also way more aggressive than previous Tekken games. It rewards going on the offensive and doesn't give you much for playing defensively, which is honestly the biggest complaint most people have with it. It's also worth keeping in mind that Tekken 8 launched on all platforms at once on day one. Tekken 7 spent two full years in arcades before it ever hit consoles, so by the time regular players got it, most of the rough edges were already smoothed out. Hence it felt more polished, it had a two year head start. Now, about all the "Tekken 7 was so much better" crowd, here's the thing. If Tekken 7 is such a masterpiece, why has it gone on sale for up to 80% off multiple times, and still never come close to matching Tekken 8's player count? Tekken 8 has consistently had more players, and that says a lot. At some point you have to ask, are people actually criticizing the game, or are they just hopping on a hate train? Because there's a difference between real feedback and just complaining for the sake of it. That said, there are real issues. The game does need more balancing, and the developers should be focusing on that instead of pushing more microtransactions. The recent patches have toned down some of the aggression on a few characters, which is a step in the right direction, but more defensive options are still needed. Look, I genuinely want this game to succeed. I want more people playing it and enjoying it. So here's my honest recommendation, if you're in a dilemma of to buy or not to buy, wait for a sale and grab it then. That's exactly what I did. But even if you buy it at full price, I don't think you'll feel like your money was wasted. You'll get your money's worth either way. For the more cautious ones though. Sale. Trust me. If you're a Tekken fan, you'll have a good time. The game isn't perfect, but it's far from the disaster some people make it out to be.

[h1]Tekken 8 — The Event Fans Have Been Waiting For[/h1]  Tekken 8 is, without exaggeration, an event fans have waited years for. The project harnesses all the power of Unreal Engine 5: characters are rendered down to the smallest detail, and their animations, along with the arenas, look absolutely stunning. But let's take it step by step.  [h2]💥 Gameplay: King of Aggression and Pressure[/h2] The developers at Bandai Namco decided to radically change the game's tempo, focusing on fierce and relentless offense. The key mechanic here is [b]Heat[/b], which can be activated once per round. This doesn't just add spectacle — it fundamentally changes the flow of battle: enhanced moves unlock, chip damage goes through block, and you can unleash a powerful attack with a unique animation. The classic "Rage" mechanic (Rage Art) is still here, allowing you to turn the tide of a fight on your last breath.  [h2]👨‍🎓 Welcome Newcomers: Special Style[/h2] The developers made sure the game is accessible to newcomers. [b]Special Style[/b] — simplified controls — lets you pull off flashy combos with basically one button. It's a great way to get a taste of the game without learning complex inputs. And if you decide to dive deep into the combat system, one of the most detailed training modes in the genre will help you perfect your skills.  [h2]👥 Roster and Content[/h2] At launch, the game features [b]32 unique fighters[/b] — a huge and diverse lineup that lets everyone find a character they love, from martial arts masters to the talking bear, Panda. And of course, with seasonal passes, Bandai Namco continues to expand the universe, adding both new and long-awaited classic characters.  [h2]🗡️ Story: An Epic Drama in the Best Traditions[/h2] The story campaign "The Dark Awakening" evokes mixed feelings. On one hand, it's epic and incredibly spectacular, playing out like a good action movie with plenty of over-the-top battles and beautiful CG cutscenes. On the other hand, it can be completed in just 2–3 hours, which for such a massive game feels lacking. But if you want to learn more about the other characters, their individual story episodes have you covered.  [h2]😟 But There's a "Fly in the Ointment"[/h2] Sadly, it's not without problems. The main stumbling block for many is [b]monetization[/b]. After release, players were outraged by the battle pass and prices for in-game items, leading to a wave of anger and a rating crash on Steam.  Unfortunately, the troubles didn't end there. The release of Season 3 in 2026, which was supposed to fix the balance, caused another wave of backlash. Players felt things only got worse.  [list] [*] Defensive mechanics were weakened, and movement efficiency was reduced. [*] The whole game, according to fans, turned into a chaotic "random attack simulator." [*] The Steam rating dropped again to "Mostly Negative" reviews. [/list] On top of that, some players still face crashes and technical errors in online mode.  [h2]⚔️ Tekken 8 vs. Competitors[/h2] When comparing Tekken 8 to its main rivals, several key points stand out:  [list] [*] [b]Graphics:[/b] Unreal Engine 5 takes Tekken 8 to a new level, leaving the visual style of Mortal Kombat 1 and Street Fighter 6 behind. [*] [b]Gameplay:[/b] Unlike more conservative fighting games, Tekken 8 commits fully to aggression. [*] [b]Accessibility:[/b] The project is perfect for beginners thanks to Special Style and extensive training. [*] [b]Content:[/b] 32 characters at launch is far more than competitors offer. [*] [b]Monetization:[/b] Tekken 8's aggressive monetization draws criticism — Street Fighter 6 handles this system more gently. [/list]  [h2]🏆 Verdict: Should You Play in 2026?[/h2] [b]Tekken 8[/b] is a true technological breakthrough for the genre — the best fighting game in the series when it comes to graphics, pace, and spectacle.  Every fighting game fan absolutely needs to play it for its incredible combat system and visual brilliance. However, as you enter this world, be prepared that on the other side of the screen you'll face not only a fierce opponent but also [b]aggressive monetization and unstable balance[/b] that the developers haven't yet managed to bring together.  [spoiler]P.S. Tekken 8 is, at its core, a fantastic fighting game that successfully modernizes the series without abandoning what made Tekken special in the first place. The new Heat system encourages aggression, the training tools are among the best the genre has ever seen, and the replay system gives players unprecedented opportunities to learn and improve. Combined with a strong roster, excellent visuals, and a surprisingly enjoyable amount of single-player content, Tekken 8 feels like a worthy successor to one of the most respected fighting game franchises ever created.  That said, Tekken 8 launched under very different circumstances than Tekken 7. Many players forget that Tekken 7 spent nearly two years in arcades before arriving on PC and PlayStation 4. During that time, Bandai Namco was able to gather feedback, fix issues, and refine character balance before the wider audience ever touched the game.  Tekken 8 had no equivalent "arcade test period." Instead, it launched simultaneously across platforms, meaning the global player base effectively became the first large-scale testing environment. The result was predictable: several characters released stronger than intended, balance issues became apparent quickly, and various bugs and interactions had to be addressed through post-launch patches.  While this led to some frustration for competitive players, it is also important context when evaluating the game's early balance. Tekken 8 was not building upon years of arcade iteration like Tekken 7 did. It was evolving in real time in front of millions of players.  Even with those growing pains, Tekken 8 succeeds because its foundation is exceptionally strong. The movement, spacing, punishment, and mind games that have defined Tekken for decades remain intact, while the new systems push the series forward in meaningful ways. It isn't a perfect game, but it is a bold and confident step into the future of Tekken, and one that demonstrates a clear commitment to both veterans and newcomers alike.

This is a review for Tekken 8's single player content and other pointless amenities, i got ♥♥♥♥ to do before i can properly start labbing as much as i wish to and even then i doubt my insights would be anything worth listening to. We love Heat, don't we folks?  My opinion on the graphics and the aesthetics in general might not be the most "technical" compared to other games i've talked about because this is by far the most modern looking game i've played since Red Dead Redemption 2 on Xbox One and my lord does it look so pretty even on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC. I cannot say for sure how this ranks against other more recent games but as far as i'm concerned Tekken 8 looks and feels incredible to play, which is such a breath of fresh air after playing Tekken 7 and its janky textures and physics.  The character design doesn't reach the heights of its predecessor, on the other hand. Characters are far from repulsive on average, mind you, but there's a lot of them that even if not downright ugly do look worse than in their recent past iterations. Paul.  The music might be my least favourite in the entire series. Sure, there's more genre variety than there was in 7's, but unlike that game i really haven't heard a single track that i would save in any of my playlists. I went out of my way to look it up on Youtube to see if maybe the game's overwhelming sound design was drowning the music, it didn't help. I suppose Storm Rising is good but i find that it's lacking a certain "punch", for lack of better words. It's just too soft for this type of game but not in an interesting way like certain tracks from past titles.   The character editor is a mixed bag. There's a few notable improvements, like being able to modify the placement of your accessories, and shoes are finally their own clothing part, but these additions come with a few downsides, like accessories once again being limited to two per character after 7's three which is very disappointing, plus you're once again limited to a single particle effect, and there just doesn't seem to be as much stuff to put on like in 7's and Tag 2's base games. I get that this is an entirely new game while Tag 2 was based off of 6 and 7 had a massive life cycle with lots of free updates, but i can't consider myself fully satisfied with what's on offer here and being able to modify pupils shape isn't gonna make me change my mind.   The main story mode of Tekken 8 was so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool, i swear to Jesus and the holy Mary.  No stupid journalist hogging the spotlight like in the past, no jarring low quality in-game cutscenes, no chapter structure that forces you to play characters that have nothing to do with the story, none of the nonsense that you're used to see here, just 5-6 hours of pure unadulterated HYPE.  All of the things i praised Tekken 7 for are back, this time with the monetary backing needed to properly realize Harada's creative vision. The gameplay is full of things that separate it from the regular CPU fights both for the sake of variety and to feel more interconnected with the story, and the quality of the CG cutscenes almost looks like something you'd see out of a movie sometimes.  The narrative does get a bit corny at times, but i'd say this overall works in favour of the many many moments that needed a bit of emotional backdrop to feel as cool as they end up being. I'm fully aware part of me is glazing this mode so hard not just because of its own strengths, but also because of how bad other games tend to be in comparison, and i don't care. I'm just glad i got to play a fighting game story that doesn't suck for the first time in so long.   And then there's the other story mode, which is worse, to say the least.  Production values not being as refined is fine given it's a free update put out to make you buy the first batch of DLC characters, but even so... Yoshimitsu, Eddie and Lidia is the most simultaneously boring and make-shift group they could have come up with, and Yoshimitsu doesn't even get any actual fights, SO WHY IS HE THERE? And that's the last question here anyone should be asking. Did they SERIOUSLY have to bring back Heihachi? You already introduced Reina which was his stand-in to keep the Mishima melodrama going, what more could you possibly do with this character? He had the perfect death in 7, leave him be. And Jun is also back, because why the ♥♥♥♥ not? And Claudio? Also not dead. He didn't get blown into nothing by Kazuya, he just dodged it and took a nap for the rest of the story. No one is ever really gone.   Arcade Quest can be seen two ways, either as a neat side-piece to the cinematic story mode that you can nib at whenever you have nothing else going on, or as its intended purpose which is to be a tool to introduce new Tekken players to competitive play, and it doesn't matter which one you prioritize because this mode is SO ass at both those things.  If you mean to get competitive, there is NOTHING here for you. You'll get taught the very basics of the mechanics once in a while which is fine enough, but that should just be the start, not the entire thing. Each of the arcades has secondary objectives in the form of specific actions that you're tasked to complete for extra stuff. While this is a decent idea and all, these objectives should have been made a lot specific and harder so that players don't just happen to mash into doing what the game asks of them. For example, having to do certain actions within a round and winning it multiple times instead of keeping count throughout all matches within the arcade, or keeping some sort of streak to reward consistency. NPCs prioritize certain patterns over others which is another good thing but it's not accentuated nearly enough. I'm not saying the mode should be too hard because that's gonna scare away those same casuals you want to bring in, but if every fight can be won in autopilot then what's the point?   And if you just want to play this for fun, everything about the way Arcade Quest presents itself is so unappealing right off the bat. Those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gross disgusting lame UGLY avatars i swear, i don't even want to imagine how much money and time went wasted putting together and animating those Wii party game shovelware abominations because if i do i'm gonna puke. And wait until you hear them talk! This mode has the most gormless Pokémon-esque dialogue you'll read in a game that isn't Pokémon itself, having every NPC being madly obsessed with the concept of Tekken and talking you down like you're a toddler somehow without actually imparting any useful knowledge that you don't already learn through the tutorials.  And the gameplay? It's regular CPU fights, that's it. In my Tekken 7 review i praised the Treasure Battle mode for how fun and addictive it is with all its gimmicks and cool stuff going on. None of that is here, getting replaced by the Super Ghost Battles.  Tekken 8 is using "the latest AI technology" to create a less charming version of what you could already do with Amiibo fighters in Smash for the WiiU, more than a decade ago, which i suppose is an accurate microcosm of AI's entire modus operandi, but i digress. It's a gimmicky idea now like it was back then, and that would be fine if they limited its presence to playing your own or other people's ghosts, but they had to go and ruin a good thing instead. Super Ghost Battles work in the same way as the old Arcade/Treasure Battles, except they removed boss battles that are unplayable outside of story mode, rule changes, streak bonuses and occasional extra rewards, all in favour of more accurate and challenging CPU fights, which is something that should have been in the main bulk of Arcade Quest, even if toned down a bit in difficulty.   Also, i don't give a dang if those modes are outdated or whatever the ♥♥♥♥, bring back Survival and Time Attack you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cowards, what the hell am i supposed to do with that basic ass Arcade mode with no bonus rounds or exclusive final boss or anything

It's disappointing because the game itself is genuinely excellent, but the cost of keeping up with everything feels unreasonable. This has been a common point of criticism among players despite the strong gameplay.  If you're only interested in the base game, you'll probably have a great time. But if you want the complete experience, be prepared to spend far more than the initial purchase price.

These days, players just keep rolling their face over their controller and their opponent has NO option but to die. Stances that transition into each other while giving plus frames (their attack recovers faster so they get to attack again first) with little to no chance to play around it and find the right way to turn the fight around. Overall, they made the game pretty, but gutted out everything that made Tekken.......Tekken........ This is not the series that I grew up with and fell in love with. I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to new players.   3/10

Later on, I went back and played Tekken 4 and Tekken Tag Tournament, then discovered that Tekken 5 included Tekken 1, 2, and 3. I was absolutely gassed. I played Tekken 6 here and there, but I didn’t get a PS3 until the PS4 era had already started, so I missed out on a chunk of the online experience back then. Even with all that, this franchise has remained incredibly solid over the years, and Tekken 8 proves that again.  You can genuinely see the graphical evolution from one game to the next, and Tekken 8 looks insane. What surprised me most is that it still runs well on my pretty outdated laptop with the right settings, which I really appreciate.  Another huge plus for me is how active the online scene is. I currently live in Nigeria, and finding matches in Tekken 7 could be rough sometimes. In Tekken 8, it’s way easier to consistently find people to play with, and that alone has made the experience so much better for me.  I’m currently Garyu rank, but I’m very much a casual player. I don’t lab for hours or study frame data, I just hop on, have fun, and enjoy the fights. And honestly, Tekken 8 is perfect for that.

If you’re new to fighting games or to Tekken 8, this game is fantastic.  It’s a lot of fun to just hit buttons and see what every character does. You can stumble into some really cool combos even with only a very basic understanding of a character’s moveset. Everything looks cool and feels satisfying to pull off.  The game also has a massive starting roster compared to other fighting games. Street Fighter 6 launched with 18 characters, Guilty Gear -Strive- launched with 15, while Tekken 8 launched with 32. Unlike a lot of other fighting games, DLC doesn’t feel mandatory because 32 characters is already more than enough variety to last hundreds of hours before you even think about spending extra money.  It includes a cinematic story mode and fully animated character arcade endings, both of which are funny and really well done. Tekken has always had some of the best story modes in fighting games because they’re cinematic without taking themselves too seriously, and Tekken 8 continues that perfectly. It also has Arcade Quest, which might honestly be one of the best learning modes ever made for a fighting game. It teaches you the complexities of the system and the characters without feeling like you’re just grinding through tutorials.  On top of that, it has the best character customization in any fighting game right now. It’s built on Unreal Engine 5, so the graphics look amazing, and the netcode is probably best-in-class for a 3D fighting game.  This is objectively a phenomenal fighting game, which is exactly why people are so mad about certain design decisions (and why the reviews are mixed).  People are frustrated with the state of Tekken 8 because it’s such an incredible game — honestly one of the best games of the decade regardless of genre — that gets held back by some really questionable balancing decisions. Tekken 8 is probably the most complete fighting game package ever released, and with just a few relatively minor tweaks, it could easily be the undisputed GOAT.  Instead, every major update feels like the balancing team sat down and mathematically calculated the worst possible design choices they could make before implementing them. It’s like someone making the greatest pizza slice you’ve ever had and then dumping anchovies all over it. Which is why the reaction has been so negative (hence the mixed rating). The emotional response to someone throwing soup on a Picasso is a lot stronger than someone throwing soup on a high school art project.  That said, until you’ve put at least 100 hours into the game, you probably won’t even really notice the impact of these balance changes. For most new players, it’s virtually unnoticeable.  TL;DR: Tekken 8 is a phenomenal game and maybe the best fighting game ever made for the first 100–200 hours. After that, some really questionable and frustrating balancing decisions start becoming noticeable.

As far as offline/singleplayer content goes, its alright, but not SF6 level. Ghost battles are pretty sweet against other player's ghosts as it really changes the AI behavior a decent bit. However I don't know that can really be considered "offline" functionality since you need to go online to download the ghosts. So really you've got the standard story mode with fights sprinkled between cutscenes, traditional arcade style "character stories" that are pretty bare bones, and a Mii-style avatar mode where you participate in a few virtual tournaments that essentially serves as an extended tutorial. The beach ball mode is an amusing diversion, so points there for the extra mode. Just not a lot of singleplayer longevity here.

SF6 has too few characters, and they really forced that custom character and “open world” mode that honestly feels unnecessary for a fighting game.  At least Tekken kept the essence it has had since the PS1 era. I believe too many innovations in fighting games can end up ruining them. Tekken brings a huge roster of characters, and even characters who are no longer tied to the story, like Heihachi and Armor King, are still playable. Meanwhile, MK prefers adding random movie and TV characters instead of keeping the franchise’s own characters, and honestly that gets tiring.  Tekken 8’s gameplay is also spectacular — smoother and faster. Even with all the complaints about easy combo mechanics for n00bs, playing online is still really fun. Another thing I loved is the character customization, being able to change hairstyles and many other things without needing mods.  Tekken 8 gets a 10/10 from me. Best fighting game out right now, and absolutely worth every penny for anyone who loves arcade-style games.

While I still have certain griped with the game, admittedly I'm still having a lot of fun with my friends when it comes to Tekken 8. Rollback is nice, the way it teaches you basics feels nice, and the Arcade Quest, despite feeling at first like it wasn't good to play at first, it does try to teach core mechanics based on who your playing with.  Personally, I still wish the story mode would allow you to play with the character you want while still getting to see cutscenes of the Mishima and the Kazama storytelling, But I get it, they want us to experience what they character must have gone through as well. And I suppose they succeeded, just took me a bit to learn the character (But to be fair, I did play it on hard instead of easy, so it's a bit on me). Meanwhile, everyone else doesn't really get much story other than like, minor parts of the story or its own Character Episode. Meaning we have to continue paying attention to interviews and shadow dropped lore on wikis for anything else.  The gameplay in and of itself is fun. And while it was rough from the get go, the controls has been simplified a lot since back then. Maybe a bit too simplified, but it's definitely very beginner friendly. From a casual perspective, it's nice if your aim is only to play for fun and not competitive. But there will be people who abuse this in competitive play surely. Other than that, all in all it can be pretty fun if you know when to take a break, desalt, and other stuff.  I do wish there was much more for customization on base game and not rely so much on battle pass. Or at the very least, if you will make battle pass exclusive items, please make sure they come back or something. As someone who joined late because I was unavailable, really wanted to get the "I hate Rich People" shirt, but it doesn't look like I can get it anymore. Not to mention, base game customization just looks so... empty compared to Tekken 5 through 7. Tekken 6 and 7 (Don't you dare make the joke) had so much customization. So much, that the optimal way to get more item was via Treasure Battle in Tekken 7, and even then, half the time, it might not be for the character you play. In here? You get the bare minimum. Want more? Invest some money in battle pass to get unlocked customization. Missed it? Sucks to be you. Battle pass just in general sucks.  Finally, the Tekken Longue and Ghost Battle. Honestly? These modes are pretty useful. Back then we only had lobby rooms back in the days. And if you weren't someone with Keyboard adapters back in console, there was little reason to use the player lobby chat box. But in Fighter Lounge where multiple people are around? It feels so natural to chat and learn with other players when attempting to play for fun or even just get to socialize with other Tekken fans. I don't think I ever socialize with other Tekken fans online. Mainly because I was worried everyone was competitive hungry but, I guess some of them are relatable to the characters in Arcade Quest. Which is a nice breath of fresh air. Some people focus more on communicating by customization, how others play, and sometimes, expressing with favorite moves of their characters. And I appreciate that. All while the Ghost mode also gives you a good idea of how those players play and potentially practice with data similar to said players. Of course,I wouldn't say Ghost Data will replace players. In my opinion, Ghost Data will play a little worse than what the actual player can truly do. But it is nice to have something to practice with.  All in all, despite I have a preference for other Tekken games, Tekken 8 is fun to play and communicate with still. Despite the things that does disappoint me.

Alright, strap in. This is a long one and you’ll realize why it had to be this long by the end of this review.  For the record, I played Tekken 3 onwards without taking it seriously. Just mashing buttons with friends, having fun, maybe learn a basic combo. Tekken 8 was the first time I actually wanted to learn the game properly. I wanted to learn movement, spacing, punishment, matchup knowledge, all the things longtime players always talk about when they say “real Tekken.”  And after spending hundreds of hours trying to learn it seriously, I came out of it seriously frustrated and depressed.  The ranked climb in this game is one of the most miserable Sisyphean experiences I’ve had in a fighting  game. See you can lose and go “Oh okay I did some mistakes there, I’ll go to the replays and learn”, but most of the characters make you lose for guessing their stance rushdown wrong. Basically, you play the casino and hope you guess them right, which is most definitely what a fighting game is all about. /s  Four points from which the misery comes from: -	Why bother learning neutral when the game keeps introducing new moves that skip neutral entirely -	Why bother learning proper punishment and movement when characters are given tools that cover multiple options at once (homing mid strings that is +8 on block and wallsplats and puts character into stance mixup which you have to guess again to not get ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ blown up to pieces) -	Learning difficult execution only to realize some characters get comparable or better reward from much easier tools (If this is any indication, Devil Jin has been nerfed to graveyard tier in this game. And no Mishima characters are top tier.) -	Dealing with a system level mechanic that massively rewards momentum and nonstop braindead monkey like offense.  And this is where Heat becomes the main problem. Heat was supposed encourage players to be more aggressive. On paper, it's a good addition. In reality, it's an absolute pain to be on the receiving end of. Idt aggression is the problem here. Old Tekken games had it's own version of aggression. The problem is that Heat gives too many things at once: •	free pressure,  •	chip damage,  •	forced guesses,  •	enhanced moves,  •	heat smashes that does close to combo damage,  •	combo extensions,  •	heat dashes,  •	and ways to stay plus while continuing offense.  Most heat moves have very little counterplay. You just have to eat it and pray to whichever god you worship you survive the ♥♥♥♥ the other player is about to serve you. Some characters (Steve, Dragunov, King, Lydia, Law) genuinely feel designed around never letting the other player play the game once momentum starts. In fact I think they purposely made EVERYONE stance rushdown character to fit into the Heat meta, which just makes everyone so... similar. There's no character identity anymore. There's no more counter hit focused characters. There's no more spacing and punish focused characters. It's just sad.  You spend time learning movement and spacing just to run into: •	heat engager into forced stance mixup,  •	plus frame stance transitions,  •	tracking mids that catch sidesteps,  •	armored approaches,  •	absurd wall carry,  •	and massive damage off mistakes that don't even feel particularly hard to execute.  And the frustrating part is that this isn't happening occasionally. This happens in every match you play. People keep saying “just learn the matchup,” but eventually you realize a lot of matchups are less about adaptation and more about memorizing layers upon layers of knowledge checks while dealing with constant forced offense. So if you're a new serious Tekken player, god help you.  A lot of rounds don't feel earned anymore. They feel snowballed. One mistake becomes launcher into huge wall carry into wall pressure with heat mix. Usually you eat a stupid heat stance mix and eat ♥♥♥♥ at 15 seconds into the round.  And because offense is so overwhelming in this game, sometimes it genuinely feels like you stopped playing 10 seconds ago and you're just waiting to die because the momentum system already decided the round.  The saddest part is that underneath all of this, there actually is a great fighting game here. There are moments where both players are moving carefully, checking spacing, whiff punishing properly, adapting to habits, conditioning each other. In those moments, the game feels incredible. You finally understand why people fell in love with Tekken in the first place.  But those moments feel interrupted constantly by mechanics that heavily reward forcing offense over carefully building advantages. And honestly, that's what disappoints me the most. I wanted to love this game. I spent hundreds of hours trying to love this game. I genuinely tried to improve instead of blaming the game immediately. But after enough hours, enough ranked sessions, enough labbing, and enough watching entire rounds disappear because someone activated Heat and started running stance pressure, I just don't think the developers actually want newer players to learn Tekken fundamentals properly anymore. It feels like they want players constantly pressing buttons, constantly engaging, constantly forcing momentum, because that's more exciting to watch. Definitely fun to watch, absolutely hair ripping anger inducing to survive.  Look, maybe that's what you want. Maybe all you want is to win with little to no learning of the game's techniques and letting your character do all the heavy lifting while your brain shuts down looking at all the pretty flashy move effects they put in.  For me, it just signals the death of Tekken as we know it.  EDIT: Okay maybe they started toning down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with heat this season 3. Good small steps in the right direction, but I still feel there's a lot to "reverse" before it feels balanced. Keep it up team, it's actually starting to feel fun to play again (sometimes). Now here's a problem with the recent Tekken game that I personally found: It has a lot of "nerfing". Unlike on how Tekken 5 and 6 remain consistent, Tekken 8 needs a patch of update to make the game appeals to the player's input, which I found it annoying when you just want to improve the way you play the game at it's core without having yourself constantly felt FOMO for no good reason before couple of days later you rant and complains a lot about how bad the recent update is. This is why a consistency of a game in a old franchise like Tekken matters, because it has a fans from a various generations of both old and new worldwide. [h1]Overall Review - 1/5[/h1]  0 - Horrible (Don’t Buy, not enjoyable at all) 1 - Bad (Generally not enjoyable, but may have some few good things about it) 2 - Average (Solid, nothing really special) 3 - Good (few flaws, but really enjoyable) 4 - Fantastic (near perfect)  5 - Perfect/Timeless (Must Buy)  [b]tldr[/b]: I have a lot to say about Tekken 8, so I don’t mind if you just read the tldr. I personally cannot give this a good review. There are too many mechanics that make it a 1 player game. Sure there may be a way to avoid it, but in my opinion, Tekken has been the game of many options. I can’t even say this is a game for casuals unless you are playing with other casuals, because the game is so one sided if you know the basic flow chart. There is no neutral with all these phantom hitboxes and full screen moves that lead to plus frames on block. Sidestep/walk feels very unreliable in a 3D game because of all the plus frames on moves. Tracking will follow you no matter what. The game is very inconsistent and is shown in all levels of gameplay. It feels like we are playing an early access of Tekken 8 and it may never come out of early access.  Firstly, I’m somewhat a veteran of Tekken. I started getting beat up by my uncle mashing in Tekken 3. I played competitively trying to learn how to play til tekken 6. I remember watching LevelUpYourGame’s tutorials and Bogus Journey. I don’t see those types of videos anymore, which is sad. I’ve competed in Tekken locals, Norcal Regional, and Evo. Over the years of playing Tekken 3, 6,Tag2, 7, & 8 I played multiple characters and learned a lot of characters. I have many pages of documentation of Tekken 7 and Tekken 8 characters. Was I good? Probably not. I would like to think that I tried to be. It all feels like I wasted my time learning, because why try to adapt when I can just be plus and continue my offense where I don’t need to learn the opponent’s character. I’m honestly tired. My friends quit and I think it is time for me too.  [h2]Pros:[/h2]  [b]Story Mode[/b] - I personally think the story is okay/good. It pretty much went full anime. Storyline finished up the whole Mishima story between Kazuya and Jin. I kinda wish some of the mechanics in the story was part of the main Game Mechanic like the quick muscle flex. I wish we could get more tekken force like a rogue-lite tekken force mode.   [b]Character Design[/b] - I do like certain characters having a mechanic like Zafina’s Anathema meter or Law having nunchucks, but I do think they went too far in terms of Game Mechanics. Nina’s gun went too far, especially the mid gun move that was safe.  [b]Netcode[/b] - This has been the best netcode Tekken has had, but it is not perfect. I would rather not go back to previous games because of this.  [b]Art/Animation[/b] - Most Triple A games are visually appealing.   [b]Sound/Music[/b] - I’m not really a music/sound person, but I think it's good from the first time I’ve played it. I honestly don’t listen to the music in the game anymore. There is a jukebox where you can switch music from older games, which is pretty cool.  [h2]Cons:[/h2]  [b]Game Mechanic (Core Mechanics, Heat)[/b] - Let's start with Heat. Heat is an oppressive mechanic that once used will give you an advantage against the opponent in almost any situation. It's bad because once you're so positive your options become minimized from maybe 4 to 1. If you guess wrong, you might end up in a Combo that does more than 50% of your health that would lead you into another 50/50 situation. You only get 1 to 2 chances to play the game if you are defending. Hitboxes on moves are ridiculously too large for the actual moves. A lot of moves like ff+2 or heat burst just hit from across the screen, which makes things never miss. Moves will track you even if you sidestep/walk. You will also get a counter hit if you try to punish a move after sidestepping. I honestly could keep going, but this review would be 10+ pages.  [b]Fighting Styles[/b] - They made it so every character plays the same. The same combos, the same moves, the same stances. All combos reach wall to wall, it doesn't matter the character. For example, a lot of characters now have a d2 that evades highs that never had them before. Characters like Jack-8, King, & Heihachi didn’t have stances. All characters are just homogenized. After a unhealthy amount of hours put into the game sweating my balls off in ranked. I feel ready to leave a review.   Pros:  - Bar to entry is low. Theres a character for people of all skill levels. Some requiring more execution and time to learn than others but there should be something for everyone.  - Practice / Replay mode has everything you'd want as a tool to get better at the game. Bonus points for the replay mode feature that lets you take control of your character at any point in time to experiment with what you could have done differently in a match.  - There are some game modes to engage with if you didn't buy the game to play ranked. The game has a 'ok' story mode, character episodes, ghost battles (AI vs AI), tekken ball and lounge to engage with for those looking for a casual experience. You can even just load up a private lobby and play for fun with friends.  Cons:  - Ranked matchmaking. Complete hit or miss but mostly misses - devs have made so many changes with the points / gain system for wins | losses but I still found myself getting one and doned alot in ranked matches. Players aren't entitled to rematches which is fine. But it sucks to win the first match of a set, lose the next and then have the opponent leave with the win with no rematch.   - The devs. Bandai themselves are the biggest threat to the game with their poor decision making and the direction they're taking tekken 8 in. With it being 2 years since launch its only now in season 3 that they've made much needed changes to characters who were overdue for a balance pass. A step in the right direction for sure but we can only watch to see what they do next.  - The microtransactions. Besides the DLC characters which are a given in fighting games these days. The rest of the store items are just ...... sad. The costumes are literal asset rips from previous games put into tekken 8 with a $7 price tag slapped on while some of the paid battle pass items are customization items that were free in Tekken 7 originally. Almost zero effort put into making anything worth buying from the store.  Overall:   I recommend the game solely on the basis that anyone can pick it up, choose a character and just play. You have have the game modes listed above to engage with if you're someone just wanting a casual fighting game. For those taking the leap and choosing to jump into ranked. I would still recommend it as the main hook of this game is your ability to learn and get better. The game has its unreal highs and brutal lows and its the hook of trying to climb the ladder on ranked that has kept me playing for hundreds of hours.

Rage Arts were already trash enough adding more hand holding in ranked just makes it worse.  Visually, the game looks great and feels smooth to play. But despite that, I find myself losing interest quickly. I’ll get on, enjoy a few matches, and then remember why I stopped playing.  It’s clear the developers are trying to attract a new audience and make the game more beginner friendly, but in doing so, it feels like they’ve taken away from what long time players enjoyed about the series. I just wish the same level of effort put into making the characters sexy, they put effort in ranked balance and overall gameplay tuning.  It’s not a terrible game, but it’s not great either and definitely not worth full price, especially if your main character isn’t even available yet. tbh im mixed. The game at its best is fun, with stellar presentation and animation work, very good performance for a game that  looks as good as it does. But its marred by lingering issues. insane jank and poor balance. every one feels like a top tier character. If youre familiar with the series it feels like every aspect of tekken but with rocket fuel added making the experience volatile. too many easy to enforce guessing games, too many prolonged safe options that force people to guess way too often which can often lead to an easy counter hit into a full combo even if you play good neutral. execution cost is significantly lower in this game for massive damage/long combos. its goofy and volatile but it can be fun but the toxic elements outstay their welcome and they are overbearing on the game. tekken 8 is fun and feels like a game that could have longevity if it wasnt hurt by some very poor decisions even after appropriate feedback.  Tekken 8 features volatile netplay and aggressive rollback making the previous issue significantly worse. You cant have an aggressively offensive game feel good if defense, sidestepping feel like it barely has an effect or if the netplay feels hit or miss or if one sided rollback becomes too invasive.   it also cant feel good for a casual/new player to need to learn an encyclopedia worth of information about different systems or move interactions per character just to approach the game because what was intended to make the game easier to approach became a tool that just amplified the offense of people that already knew the game, and so it gives more experienced players an easier way to apply significantly more oppressive knowledge checks than before. For the hardcore player it can't feel good because the options you do have that are better reward are not very consistent (ie sidestep punishing) or way too risky to pull off because offense has such strong tracking and clippable hitboxes that only get janky with rollback so the safest thing to do is to block most the time in a 3d FIGHTER which is supposed to have 3D movement as a way to enhance the offense and defense.   when someone DOES make a good read it can just end up with the player being put back into a blender very quickly with little being offset to the aggressor, most characters can blow you up very easily and just blast through the tug of war of neutral. also the DLC are insanely overpriced and not always good value. the battlepasses take very long to progress and the rewards are just bad for the money. the shop items are also mostly bland or recycled. A pair of shoes that are distinct to one characters outfit at base is something you can money to have access to for every other character but only if you pay more. You have to BUY the DLC characters in order to lab the matchups. Replay function allows you to get a rough idea, but its not a full replacement for labbing.  in all fairness the recent 3.01 and 3.02 are some of the best patches this game has received and has toned down the more oppressive elements of the game noticeably which was mainly heat, chip damage and many plus on block mix ups. Its a good direction that they need to continue in and hopefully increase execution requirements of high value low risk moves. Right now the worst problem with tekken 8s balance is how strong being able to blow up neutral is and how easy it is to convert into full high damage combos. What used to take more practice back in the day can be done with half as much effort and thats both good and bad, good for newcomers that want a flashy satisfying fighting game, bad for those that develop experience and want some nuanced gameplay.

Tekken has sadly become about little more than juggling. The aim is to make sure your opponent doesn't get to do anything, not because you play better...but because you just happened to land a launch first and they can't respond while being tossed around like a ball. Not only is it dull to be tossed around like a ball or to be tossing the ball instead of, you know, actually fighting...it very disproportionately favours some characters who have very easy launches to land and very easy follow up combos for juggling.  The heat mechanic makes the above issue even worse. There have been some adjustments to lessen the issue but it frankly has not been anywhere near enough.   It is also astonishing that something as strong as a Rage Art is a one button press. It does enormous damage, as much as a long combo, and it is very easy to land. In lower ranks it is used as a massive crutch by players who are not good at trades.   I still play the game but only very casually among friends. I was going to try to get high ranks, but even with a high winrate I'm just not having fun because the game is all about juggling. I want to fight. Not bounce my opponent around like they're a basketball. I became bored and frustrated. Until the power of juggling is massively reduced I cannot recommend this game to anyone who actually enjoys the "fighting" in fighting games.

Man Tekken 8 is just something else entirely. I have been playing this series since the early days on Playstation 1 but this new entry feels like the developers finally just said let’s go absolutely nuts and see what happens. The first thing that hits you is the visuals because they are genuinely gorgeous and the shift to Unreal Engine 5 was clearly the right move. The characters look so detailed that you can see the sweat and the muscles tensing up during those slow motion finishes that the series is famous for. The Heat system is the real game changer though. It makes every round feel like a high stakes action movie because it rewards you for just being aggressive and staying in your opponents face. I used to be a bit more defensive and wait for an opening but now the game basically yells at you to get in there and start swinging. It feels visceral and punchy and when you land a Heat Smash it just feels so satisfying. The impact sounds and the particle effects make every hit feel like it has actual weight behind it which is something Tekken has always done well but they really peaked here. I also have to talk about the story mode because it is absolutely ridiculous in the best way possible. It is pure martial arts soap opera madness. Seeing Jin and Kazuya settle their family issues by basically destroying entire cities and throwing literal skyscrapers at each other is peak gaming. It does not take itself too seriously but at the same time you can feel the heart behind it. They even brought back a bunch of legacy stuff that made me feel super nostalgic. And if you are new to the series they finally added a way to actually learn how to play without needing a PhD in fighting games. The Arcade Quest mode is actually a really cute way to teach you the basics while making you feel like you are part of that old school arcade culture. Plus the Replay and Tips feature is probably the smartest thing I have ever seen in a fighter because the game literally pauses your own replays and tells you hey you should have punished this move with this specific button. It makes getting better feel like a natural progression instead of a chore. The roster is also solid as hell right now. You got the classics like Paul and Law who still feel great but the newcomers like Victor and Azucena bring such a fresh vibe to the mix. Playing as Victor feels like you are playing a high tech John Wick and Azucena is just fun because of her movement and the whole coffee obsession thing. Even the stages are more interactive now with walls breaking and floors collapsing which keeps you on your toes. The online play has been pretty smooth for me too which is a huge relief because bad netcode can ruin a fighting game so fast. Doing crossplay with friends on different consoles is seamless and the lobby system is actually fun to hang out in. It feels like a genuine community. Honestly if you have even a slight interest in fighting games you need to pick this up. It is loud and colorful and aggressive and just pure fun. It feels like a celebration of everything that makes Tekken great while pushing the genre forward into something that feels truly modern. I have put so many hours into this already and I still feel like I am barely scratching the surface of what I can do with my main characters. It is easily one of the best fighting games released in the last decade and I cannot wait to see how the pro scene evolves with these new mechanics. Just go buy it and start smashing buttons you will not regret it.
