I understand they want a more offensive style to tekken but they did nothing to keep defence relevant. In this game consistency is everything, if you have the option between a situational move or a consistent one, you will always pick consitent. That being said, you will find attacking is consistently the best choice, which is obviously the intention. However in this games case they take things too far. Defense is less rewarding than offense and I believe that Tekken should be this way, being able to turn the tide of the game should be a difficult thing. However it should be an expression of skill. In this game the longer you defend the more you put yourself at a disadvantage, and more often than you should you end up challenging a 50/50 as you have no opening against certain players and characters. There are just too many match ups that exploit being able to stay on the offensive consistently.   You can skip to the conclusion if you don't feel like reading all of this.  Offensive tools  -Heat smash, massive plus frames on block essentially free pressure. Counter play includes, stepping, grabbing, power crush. However some heats aren't steppable and you need to be careful of grabs some may be too slow. If hit you take anywhere between 40-60 damage which is roughly quarter health. Low heatsmashes can be blocked and punished with jab or while standing as long as its less than 14 frames, Paul might be an exception to this.  -Chip damage, essentially free damage for applying pressure, heat smash chips and so do many other moves the most drastic ones have high frames so you can usually deal with those. Many of these attacks have push back, some are also positive. This is basically giving you a passive advantage as long as you can out pressure. Counter play is to just defend, chip damage can be regenerated on counter attack however the push back can make it extremely difficult to punish in a few scenarios  -Heat engage/dash, a tool that allows you to activate heat and extend pressure. Here is where you are most likely locked into playing defence, stepping is also an option however I find I usually step early.   -Extended combos and wall carry, many characters can carry a player cross map to a wall allowing for extra damage, combo extension via wall splat and pressure by simply having an opponent against the wall. Now juggling and wall carry has always been a thing in tekken however this is just ridiculous. In my opinion this issue needs to be addressed the most.   -Guard Break, this is also nothing new typically used mid string or just when an opponents holding b. These were in tekken 7 as well, don't have much to say about it honestly duck or step depending on the attack. These can ignore reversals   -Launchers, these are essentially combo starters, should be used on block or whiff punish used to start a counter attack into big damage. Handful of unbalanced launchers, generally not a big deal.  -Power crush, hyper armored attack that deals more damage than most attacks. Can be stopped with a grab, low, duck or step. There are definitely more power crushes than in tekken 7 however there is plenty of counter play so the frequency doesn't change affect the game much if anything it allows for more options against heat smash as it can be crushed.  -Homing attacks, a blue sweeping animation means that an attack can hit while opponent is stepping no matter which direction. This is useful when your opponent is stepping often or even crouching if its a mid. Other attacks have partial homing which can lead to some weird 50/50 situations sometimes, many characters have a weak side however with the amount of attacks that can be put out especially after a heat engage, stepping is not an option as often as it should be.   -Grabs are now homing which is an interesting choice. I don't like the change honestly and I am a King main so it definintely benefits me the most. It just makes stepping weaker, which stepping is still good. I  just see no reason to nerf it like this when everything else is so ridiculously strong.   Defensive Tools  -Low parry, tool to punish opponent for predictable lows or even slower lows such as snakes edge. Learn to pick up a combo after a low parry last thing you want is landing a jab and then turtling. Has its risks, you can miss time it or even be faked out certain lows can be cancelled into a stance. Overall decent defensive option.   - Reversals allow you to grab an arm or leg reversing the opponents attack, these are not universal amongst characters nor attacks. Meaning fe characters have them, and they don't counter all attacks. Chickening which is basically a counter reversal has been removed I don't find this to be a big deal. It was seldom used and would just be an extra gimmick for attackers. Reversals are unsafe usually safer to block.  -Counter hit, moves that when timed correctly stagger, launch, or deal bonus damage. These are the defensive attack options outside of jabs and built in parries. These are good options to counter spam, pressure, and even zoning depending on the situation. Its by far the most reliable defensive option making it the strongest.  -Stepping, whether its a side step or a back dash these moves are the main alternative to block. Meaning its the imediate response to an attack along with block. Most good players won't leave themselves very negative on block meaning they get another opening or 50/50. Stepping is most usefull when your opponent has commited to a string as you can crouch and while standing punish, throw a low, side step. Or they miss a big move such as a power crush, guard break or a heat smash.   - Wall jump allows you to use the stage wall to make a counter attack. Its a very cool thing but you have probably never seen it. The reason is because its really bad, just block or get away from the wall. This is also another form of defensive attack. Now im not saying it should be nearly as useful as counterhit but I do believe they should make this a stronger option for wall escape. I personally think that they should look into reworking this feature. Many rounds are lost simply because your opponent has you at the wall. There is usually no escape unless you commit a hard read, which is just guessing at that point. The wall is definitely the most oppressive thing in this game. If they were to make it so that it can't be taken out of its animation, meaning you are guaranteed to hit. You wouldn't take reduced damage like a power crush but would retain your attack like one. Hitting your opponent and then being able to push off them either away or towards the wall. Naturally this would be a high attack and you could just block or counter hit, if you are throwing jabs you could likely still get damage in before blocking. It wouldn't make the move that much better but its something.  I have ranted long enough about this game. Overall the main issue is that pressure is the name of the game. The faster attacker gets more attacks in, more attacks means more passive chip damage and more 50/50s. Who ever is defending needs to make a hard read to turn the game around but they are already down health so the 50/50 is less favourable to them damage wise, deal a third of their health or risk dropping to 30 health. Some characters even when on the counter attack are simply less effective whether it be inferior damage, speed, or wall carry. While other characters are superior in these categories while having relatively similar frame data if not better. Making them less punishable, and more punishing at the same time. This is my first Tekken game. I'm a big fan of fighting games, and while the learning curve is relatively easy, it's not until you become familiar with the game that you realize there's a noticeable imbalance between the characters and their movesets.  While some characters have exaggerated mobility, others have enormous hitboxes, and still others have attacks that even a sidestep can't save you from. I'm not afraid of a good challenge; what bothers me is how often I feel the game forces you to take offensive initiatives instead of rewarding players for technical knowledge and actually "using their heads."  There comes a point where it might be my fault if an Eddy deletes me the first time by mashing the 3 button, but when my character has almost no attacks that take fewer frames than his spam combo, it becomes frustrating.  That said, when you find people in ranked who are truly skilled, it's incredible to see how versatile each character's tools can become and how fun it is to familiarize yourself with and learn each enemy's builds. The challenge and difficulty really do feel motivating.  If it weren't for the fact that I can only get one match every 10 minutes where there are no other players on my server, and my connection gets rejected despite being wired, just because I have 4 bars instead of 5 (simply due to latency, since almost all my games have 0 rollback and 40-50 ping).  Perhaps I'm not the most qualified person to speak like the veterans, but I'm sure this game has so much more to offer, but it's headed in the wrong direction. I was very excited for Tekken 8. I put a couple thousand hours into Tekken 7, followed TWT closely, got involved with the community, and the lead-up to this game genuinely felt special. The marketing was great, the reveal was great, and from the beta onwards I did have a lot of fun with it.  On a casual level, I still think Tekken 8 does a lot right. It looks fantastic, feels fast, hits hard, and is immediately more exciting than a lot of fighters if you just want to pick a character and start throwing hands. There is also more to do than just grinding ranked, which helps a lot. If you can get it cheap and just want something to play with friends, family, or on the couch now and then, I can absolutely see the appeal.  My problem is with what this game becomes once you want to put more time into it.  The competitive side of Tekken 8 has felt messy for too long. Ranked and matchmaking have been repeatedly reworked, including major changes in April 2025 and again in March 2026 to how matches are made, how points are gained and lost, and how rank resets work. That does not make the climb feel stable or rewarding.  Then there is the post-launch support around it. The Tekken Shop and Fight Pass were added after launch, and the Steam page now openly lists in-game purchases alongside a big stack of paid DLC. On top of that, things like disconnect penalties only arrived in December 2024, which is the kind of thing ranked should have had locked down much earlier, if not with release as these are recurring issues from previous titles. Bandai Namco has had to admit in official patch notes that some of its responses were insufficient and that certain bugs were causing significant disadvantage to players.  That is what makes this so frustrating. Tekken 8 is still fun. It is still fun to watch, it is still fun in short bursts, and I still respect that they are willing to experiment instead of just making Tekken 7.5. But if you are someone looking for a long-term competitive game to invest your time into, I do not think it feels good enough, stable enough, or well-handled enough to recommend right now.  I want to love it, but I can’t recommend it.

An excellent addition to the time-honoured fighting series, Tekken 8 is a continuation of everything that made the past iterations popular and moves the series ahead, adding modern gameplay and visuals. The game by Bandai Namco Entertainment is simultaneously familiar and new.  Presentation is one of the largest attractions of the game Tekken 8. Using the Unreal Engine 5, the graphics have become exceptionally well-detailed, with characters being created almost realistically, able to express their faces, with active stages capable of shifting during a fight. There is a living sense of the environment, and each punch, kick, and combo is visually satisfying. Such a degree of polish renders it one of the most attractive fighting games available at present.  They have even perfected the gameplay by putting on a new system (the Heat System) that promotes aggressive play and not defensive turtling. This system enables players to inflict chip damage and prolong combos, which results in making fights more aggressive and quicker. Although original Tekken enthusiasts will still feel that they are playing the familiar tricks and triggers such as juggling and perfect timing, all new upgrades would enable the game to be played by beginners without depriving the experienced players of the depth.  The genre of the tales in question, the Dark Awakening, is an extension of the ancient feud between the Mishima family and, in particular, a feud between Jin Kasama and Kazuya Mishima. It is also an action-filled and cinematic film and appears like an interactive film at other occasions. Ok...It's a positive report, but I think neutral is a fairer and accurate review of this title.  I have put almost 50 hours in at time of review, and feel like I have seen what the game offers and how it fares against predecessors and current competition.    In a nutshell; if you don't take this title as a serious, balanced online fighter, then you will have plenty of fun here.    It has all the Tekken bells and whistles - ludicrous single player campaign, goofy self-awareness and lots of sizzle in front end graphics.  But the balance between fighters really isn't there.  Power creep is  a thing with all DLC and patch updates, but fundamentally, there is a disconnect between critical character offence and punishing defence that makes games very one-sided and fast.  I've read many other accounts online and I agree that this is a sincere flaw in online competition - certainly the greater part of the game as most experience it.   Each match hinges on who gets in their juggle first, then spams attacks until the "defender" rag dolls to zero health.  Even getting in a block depreciates so much health that it is a fast battle of attrition as blows reign down on the hapless avatar.  For the player winning-it is a formula unwise to stray from; for the receiver - the match is over once they are ever on the defensive.  If you can accept that significant dynamic; there is much to like in this game.   The games are very fast for typical Tekken fare-often making it difficult to gauge a response or deflection.  This may turn away fans of the series to a degree, but I applaud the developers for trying something a little different with a predictable formula.  It just doesn't help as much as you might hope; as the matches are dependent on early connection/blunder and they may as well be even shorter for all the response a player can give.  I am not a strong competitor - but currently stand at a PB of 64% win/loss ratio: simply because I happen to luck first contact with an unblockable and bulldoze along.  I cannot even begrudge other players spamming their own small set either.  It really becomes obvious as you climb the ranks of upper tier combat levels and invariably find players repeating the same signature combo set ad nauseum because it is just how their character breaks guard best.  I just think that rinse and repeat, mapped and unblockable aggression doesn't help build or maintain a player-base.     Care has been taken to keep the hallmarks of each legacy character intact, and there is a lot of celebration in the season unlockables that are placed fairly and evenly on the ladder to access them with reasonable casual play.   Tekken Ball is fun, if a little clunky - but I like the style of it and am glad it is in here.   Customisation options are decent - not overwhelming and inexpensive to access most with in-game currency over all characters and player cosmetics. Sound on some of the levels is among the best I've heard in this style and generation of fighter - from lifting beach-funk to psychedelic opera.  The option to include music from past titles in the series throughout is my favourite extra in any fighting game, period.  The Jukebox function pulls me in where the calibre or availability of fighter might be lacking - and they put this idea to fantastic use in the climax of the single-player campaign.   So that's it - a fun game if you enter into it with eyes open - your character may have 300 moves, but you will most likely use the same 7 or 8 on repeat to be competitive with the online community doing precisely the same thing.  As a casual fighter; there is plenty to love and the fast, short content match style makes it a solid entry point for newcomers to the genre and series.  I just wish it could engage with the more seasoned gamer playerbase like it clearly intends.

Absolutely unreal situation going on with the devs (Season 3 "Back to Basics"). Been watching videos from FGC/Tekken cc's and from what it looks and feels like, this is a masterclass in what NOT to do in PR. Not recommending based on principle and the fact that this level of miscommunication-into-delulu blame-shifting* sets an awful precedent and example for other games and devs, and it's just so sad to see happen as a fan of games made with passion by developers who have their player in mind.  *(4:08, "How Season 3 Killed Tekken 8" by BoogardMG on YouTube, for direct context)  It's a big mistake to assume that a "niche" or "deep" game cannot reach a greater audience without becoming average; it is the niche that attracts the average. Make your longtime playerbase happy, and they will rave until you reach 1mil players for a few months (like with Monster Hunter). The moment you go for average, the game loses its identity and everything falls apart, and as a lifelong enjoyer of all sorts of games, that just sucks to see with so many awesome franchises and dev teams. Fortnite didn't win big because it copied Fortnite.  Another way to look at it: if videogames are supposed to be art, and you assume that real fans are happy with just being able to see the "vision of the creator(s)," don't be surprised when they roll their eyes and walk away when you present them with a work composed only of a white background and red letters that spell out "you just don't understand."   Of course no one understands; you're playing whack-a-mole with the people who showed up, until you hit a "balance" of "features" that keep certain "player demographics" that appear as though they overlap with the everyone's favorite cash-cow buzzword: "average gamer." Unfortunately, this whole ideal is psychotic in a number of ways, but mostly because it's fundamentally disconnected from the actual players here, who have been giving every bit of information needed to create a masterpiece that they would love to support. It's a hard truth to face, but it will have to be faced at one point or another by one of these big big companies before a new business precedent is set towards embracing what they've got; maybe it starts here, maybe it doesn't.   In any case, I'm pretty new to Tekken and I have fun playing with friends. But I was attracted to the game for the reasons the longtimers loved it; not because I could force my friends into shallow, unskippable cutscenes and "super" with a button, but because it seemed like there was a lot of fluidity and depth to the 3d neutral game (which created the tension that was fundamental to player expression, and thus the emotional impact of actually capitalizing well on openings and converting hits into expressive combos). Now is the perfect time for a success story, so I hope things get to turn around before it's too late, for the fans, and because it would just be cool to see.

I said I would write this review once I reached Fujin/Raijin to be at the player base "average" in Season 2. I made it to Raijin with Xiaoyu after 157 hours on Steam (in general, not only online play).  I think Tekken 8 is a great game; even with its serious balance issues, it’s definitely a very fun game if you plan to play it casually with or without friends in offline modes or Online Casual matches. The story mode is entertaining, although the narrative is quite "meh"; there is a sub-story helping you get familiar with the game mechanics and doing a decent job of teaching you the basics. You have character episodes serving as fun "what ifs." The graphics are incredible, unlike Tekken 7, which I never liked graphically. As always, the roster does not disappoint; it’s quite varied, and you’ll likely find something to your liking. New mechanics like Heat definitely add an extra layer of depth to the game in every sense, though they create certain balance problems...  The dilemma starts precisely when you begin investing time into improving, as you realize (as of this writing) every character on the roster is quite powerful, but there are definitely SEVERE problems with at least 10 characters (Anna, Bryan, Hwoarang, Asuka, Clive, Lidia, etc.). Many characters were given 50/50s through either stances or specific moves. Heat Burst creates forced 50/50 situations; therefore, the game is EXTREMELY AGGRESSIVE and based on guessing. There are too many moves offering high reward with zero risk. Many strings in the game realign their attacks if you try to sidewalk or sidestep. Combos are incredibly long, leaving you perhaps 15 seconds without actually playing while you watch a cinematic. There are attacks with full-screen range, characters losing their identity, and their weaknesses being removed.  All of this ends up creating feelings of frustration because, on some occasions, you will lose simply because you didn't guess correctly, even if you know the matchup. So, if you were thinking of playing Tekken 8 with the idea of playing a fighting game without so much BS, you should look elsewhere, as this and other balance issues are the game's biggest problem.  [h3] UPDATE: [/h3]  I delayed writing this review for 6 months because of Season 3, and oh boy... At first, I was going to give it a recommendation because, as the patches went by, they were slowly fixing the errors of Season 2. But with Season 3, the devs are clearly completely out of touch with community feedback. It’s understandable the game has an aggressive focus—at the end of the day, that’s the general direction of the game (obviously, they weren't going to remove Heat as many delusional expected). But legitimately, defense is a nightmare, and this patch only reinforced how the game wants to go down the path of mindless button-mashing and abandoning the defensive play characterizing Tekken for so long. Don’t get me wrong, Anna, Bryan, and Asuka received their well-deserved nerfs, but then you buff characters like Law? Alisa? Jun? Or you give buffs to compensate for nerfs, as in the case of Jin and others?  The game doesn't need new moves; it doesn't need to make offense "easier," as the patch notes say. The game NEEDS defensive options—ways to counter all these mix-ups, stance transitions, 50/50s, and plus-frame moves everywhere. I’m sorry, they had a whole year of feedback, and this is what we got. Truly a "Back to basics."  Despite the fact I love Tekken 8 as a video game, I cannot recommend a game where the devs have no connection to the players and their feedback. Plus, Harada abandoned the project.  Buy it if it’s stupidly cheap and you plan to play casually with friends. If you plan to invest a lot of time into ranked, the game will probably start becoming unbearable from Blue Ranks onwards.

You’ll often get caught in long, repetitive juggles that are impossible to escape. While it’s true that you can deal similar damage in just a few hits yourself, constantly being stuck in extended combos is frustrating and takes away from the experience.  The core issue is that offense feels overwhelmingly strong, while defense feels underdeveloped. You can mash your combos and buttons and of course there are counters to it, but those are often tied to coin flip guesses or the like, mindlessly attacking has just way more benefits to it. Blocking often turns into a guessing game, and if you guess wrong, you can end up stuck in a combo for what feels like 30 seconds just sitting there, unable to act, wondering what you could have done differently.   If you play with friends and you all just care about learning the game without trying to juggle the enemy from 100 - 0 then the game is actually fun. [hr] [b]* DISCLAIMER *[/b] This review has some length to it. Originally a word salad reaching the 8,000 character limit, but trimmed down to the best of my ability. [b]* END DISCLAIMER *[/b]  [h3]TLDR[/h3] [b]~600 hours. Learning matchup knowledge feels optional. Pressing first does not. Do not recommend.[/b] [hr] [h3]Review[/h3] [i]At the time of writing this review, I have accumulated 434.16 hours on Console and 162.6 hours on PC (much of PC spent locally with friends). The name on both accounts is "Hit the Apex" on Xbox (2RR8-TtY3-t79M) and Steam (38Qy-jJ2H-fFe4). Gamertag is "RagePlyr 13".[/i]  I spent nearly 600 hours combined in this game trying to learn.  Demoralizingly feels like I have nothing to show for it.  I am not afraid to admit that I am a bad player, decent at best.  This review comes from a newcomer's perspective: I had a total of 3 hours and 10 minutes messing around in training mode on Tekken 7 in 2020 and virtually no fighting game experience prior to buying this game in Winter 2024.  My first experience with Tekken 8 was on a friend's laptop in Fall 2024.   I picked Kazuya for my first match (odd choice, I know) where my inefficient movement made something click.  Backdashing. Spacing. Whiff punishing.  It felt rewarding.  So I kept playing.  I learned how to perform EWGF. I learned how to wavedash. I met a God of Destruction Lee from France named "Classy" in Season 1 and won a few matches against him in Season 2 despite being Fujin rank (on console).  Fighting him felt like a serendipitous dance...  Watching Tekken 8 devolve over time has been genuinely depressing:  [list] [*][b]Season 1:[/b] A flawed foundation built on "aggression" Bandai Namco worryingly emphasized.  [*][b]Season 2:[/b] The infamous "Defensive" patch that added more tracking moves that negated the eagerly requested sidestep buffs.  [*][b]Season 3:[/b] Lastly, the equally disappointing "Back to basics" marketing scheme that mimics much of Seasons 1 and 2. At this point, this Season should be dubbed as Season 2.5 accompanied with the phrase "Back to BS" or "Back to (Compensation) Buffs". [/list]  [h3]Closing Thoughts[/h3] It is a travesty through and through. There exists a universe where Bandai Namco listens to player feedback and reduces the amount of + frames and safe on block homing mids present in every update.  Sadly, we are not in that universe.  [b]The game incentivizes pressing. Not actual matchup knowledge.[/b]  Why sidestep when you can just block... or better yet, press first?  Learning the game feels optional. Pressing first does not.  It's a sprint to initiate tracking 50/50s until someone loses. (I have. Plenty.)  Is it due to live service elements prioritizing profits? Is it the inconsistent/bipolar game direction?  Concerningly, it feels like even the balance team doesn't know anymore.  The only "identity" left of this game will be unnecessary particle effects and egregious microtransactions in a fully priced AAA product.  [b]DO NOT RECOMMEND Especially in its current state.[/b] [hr]

As a long-time Tekken player, this is the first time I’ve found myself genuinely puzzled by the direction the development team is taking. At this point, the only elements that still feel recognizably Tekken are the character skin and legacy aesthetics; the underlying mechanics and overall game design feel increasingly inconsistent and unfocused.  What’s particularly frustrating is the widening gap between what is communicated and what is actually delivered. The game suffers from a lack of polish, with persistent bugs, uneven balancing, and features that feel either incomplete or misrepresented.  The seasonal messaging highlights this disconnect quite clearly: - Season 2 “buffed defense” -  it leaned heavily in the opposite direction. - Season 3 “back to basics” - again, the execution suggests anything but.  At this point, the pattern feels less like iteration and more like contradiction. The result is a growing sense that the vision for the game is not just evolving, but uncertain.  For a franchise with such a well-established identity, that lack of clarity is more than disappointing. It’s difficult to reconcile.

I'm writing this because I genuinely believe this could be a good fighting game. I also believe that the devs want this to be a good fighting game. Whether it be a divided philosophy among the team on where Tekken should go, interference from Bandai Namco, or a shortage of available staff members, I'm willing to give the devs the benefit of the doubt.  Unfortunately, this is where I must insert my criticisms of the game (At least for the current state it is in). I must admit that I am not a pro by any means nor am I anywhere close to being at a pro's level. My rank in the last season was Bushin for those curious. This game has fundamental problems that, since Season 1 if I'm being honest, hold the game back a tremendous amount. The Heat system is incredibly strong for some characters and basically useless on others. Nothing about Heat makes Tekken more interesting from a gameplay standpoint. Often times, Heat just makes rolling the other person easier if anything. Even entering Heat is not interesting since going into Heat is either whenever you hit a combo or land a heat engager. There's never a reason as to why you wouldn't go into Heat whenever you can. Heat is not fun to interact with nor is it fun to be on the receiving end of it. I won't even mention how this newest update was marketed in the last patch. "Back to Basics" they said. Should you wish to dive deeper into how bad this patch is, PhiDX made a great video covering the major problems as did MainManSwe. I think my biggest issue with the patch is how they seem to be changing the foundation of some characters. My prime example is Lee. I won't get into specifics, but Lee was a character I was actually considering maining. However, because of how the team is slowly shifting him from a keepout character to a character with great keepout AND offensive pressure, it makes the character dull and uninteresting to me.  I'm hoping that the Tekken team can pull a 180 and turn this game around like how SFV did, but as for right now I'm not interested in supporting Tekken 8 anymore.

So I want to say that despite me not recommending this game, that I actually really enjoy a lot about Tekken 8. The visuals and sound design are some of the best in any fighting game out there currently. And as this being my first ever Tekken game, I do love playing a lot of it. Climbing the ranks from Orange to Blue rank at the end of S2 and learning and feeling myself improve more and more was some of the most fun I've have in any fighter.  But this S3 opening patch as truly disappointed me. And it's not because I think it's as bad as others are saying, but because it really is the straw that broke the camel's back for many people. The devs lied.  Again. Just when they got our hopes up and showed signs of great character design with every DLC character past Anna and seeming like they wanted to cut back on what made S2 S2, they double down yet again. They keep prioritizing buffs over nerfs and dumbing the characters down more and more. For the first time in any fighter, I felt kinda insulted that my character, Leo, got buffed. In that, they basically changed a counter hit property on the opponent with certain moves. Moves that formerly on counter hit, you could learn a tech that would give you a small combo, but only if you learned the tech. Now? They just give it to you, no tech required.  As a newer player, That change is specifically targeted towards me. And I dislike it. I would have loved to learn that tech, get BETTER with my character. But now I'm handed it for free with no need to lab or anything. That is not fun. I felt robbed of something that would have made me a better player. And that's something they continue to do again and again and again. Across the board. On top of defense getting less and less clear and already overbearing and annoying characters becoming even more so.  There were some good changes, but the devs continue to be confused in their vision for the balance of this game. And if they're not confused, they're at the very least intentional in their decision to continuously dumb down everyone to the point that the skill ceiling and character expression is going to be looking the same amongst everyone. And isn't that the entire point of a 3D fighter over a 2D? The expression of options? The more clear shows of skills?  Unlike the popular opinion, I don't believe this game is a "party game" now. No, this is still a fighting game and there's still the existence of footsies and small Tekken (though who knows how much longer those will exist at this point). There's tons to always improve on, and I'll still keep trying to improve. I'll still find the fun in this game. I'll still keep labbing and holding out some semblance of hope that it can get better. But as of now, I understand the sour taste in everyone's mouth and understand if many others drop the game entirely. Until the devs show clear signs that they want to listen to us, or unless T8's all or nothing aggression is your cup of tea,  Just skip it for now. Virtua Figter 5 REVO is amazing if you need a 3D fighter fix, it's far and away the better alternative.

I wanted to give the devs a chance to show if they know how to properly balance a fighting game and become better at developing the game further while absorbing community critical feedback.  Turns out... they cant balance a fighting game or act on community feedback. Overtuned characters, bugs, glitches, and blocking community members for legit critiques.   From what Im seeing from the devs, they intend on Tekken 8 being a game of Oppressive Offense or "Mash For Your Life". Defending yourself in this game doesnt mean blocking, it means pressing a better, faster, stronger combination of buttons in hopes of landing something and taking advantage of every frame within that moment. Success in this game partially requires you to stay away from certain characters and pick the more top tier ones (Anna, Nina, Brian, King, etc). As Ian Fleming said in Goldfinger:  - Once is happenstance. Twice is coincidence. Three times is enemy action.  While qualifying Bamco as "enemy" might be a little on-the-nose, the idea applies to this game. In Season 1, people found this game's aggression to be overtuned. They promised Season 2 patch to be a "defensive patch". Season 2 arrived, and it was overwhelmingly aggression and new moves in the patch notes. We complained and were disappointed, and waited almost a full year to receive a proper balance patch despite the blatant balance issues that were not addressed, or even explicitly made worse; Bamco announced "back to basics" for Season 3. Turns out back to basics meant recycling old moves to fill in any remaining character weaknesses and buff aggression even more.  At this point, it should be abundantly clear that Bamco has no intention to change their direction, despite the lies they've told the playerbase for the last 2 years saying the opposite. If you like the current state of Tekken 8, then you should be happy with the game for the foreseeable future. If you think aggression should be toned down and the game is frustrating, or you're a long-time Tekken fan, then this game is not for you, and you should expect the game to keep going in the same direction it has since release.  This franchise has so much personality and skill expression, but Bamco seems to think the identity should be stripped in order to make way for a more "modern" experience to attract more casual players. No one is blaming Bamco for trying to expand its playerbase, and no one is complaining that accessibility has improved; people are unhappy because this accessibility comes at the expense of the identity and nuance that made this franchise so great.  TL;DR: wasted potential, dishonest developers, frustrated playerbase; this game and franchise are doomed and Bamco is happy about it.

In many fighting games, learning the answer to a lot of "cheap" or annoying strategies makes them something you can consistently deal with. In this game, the answer is quite often "you just have to guess," and guessing wrong twice can lose you the round. Guessing correctly doesn't even necessarily have any reward, either. Fighting games are a tough beast. A niche genre, 1v1, that normally takes plenty of time to get good at. Many times devs have tried to appeal to a more casual audience and alienated their core fanbase. Tekken 8 is no different.  Tekken 8 has had a rocky history. Season 1 had questionable designs, Season 2 was universally panned, and now Season 3 has arrived. One thing has shone through: their commitment to making the game "easier." But they have done so in a flawed way, and in turn have made a game for no one except the addicts.  Tekken can't be made completely accessible. The game has many characters, most having 100+ moves. Yet each new season, rather than attempting to trim the fat, instead adds new moves making the game even harder to learn. This is of course on top of the fact that casuals don't care for balance patches: they don't care you changed frame data to make a move punishable because they might not even know what a punish is. On top of that, Tekken 8 has favored offense to a dizzying degree, making it more and more accessible and harder to deal with as if they are making a single-player game. Problem being, this game is a fighting game: at some point, you will have to defend against this offense. Same for character weaknesses: these weaknesses have been constantly patched out, homogenizing the cast on top of making them hard to play against.  On top of all this, fighting games are often a genre that includes learning. Yet the devs want to make a game where a player who has played 20 hrs can completely threaten one that has played 200 hrs. This might sound fine on paper, but it begs the question: why bother trying to get better if the devs so clearly wish to get rid of the advantage of experience? Why bother playing for 200 hrs if you are the best you can be at 20?  Tekken 8 is a game that hates if you try and learn it. Its being designed for people who have no interest in it, and likely never will. With what the devs have shown, there is no hope for this game: they are set in their ways and no amount of backlash will change the course. Likely the only hope is if this backlash is heard for Tekken 9, if it even comes out.

TL;DR The devs ignore player feedback at nearly every turn, and will flat-out lie to the players while continuing to make asinine changes to the game that no one asked for, with almost no regard to the balance of the game.  In season 1 there were clear problems with the game. Those problems were eventually addressed, and many QoL improvements were made to heat and other aspects of the game. S+ tier characters were rightfully nerfed. Players were pretty satisfied with those changes. It was, from my perspective, commonly agreed that toning down character strength across the board, and buffing defensive options, would leave the game in a GREAT place. Devs said that it would be, and im paraphrasing here, a "defense focused patch".  And then season 2 dropped, and it IMMEDIATELY became clear that they were lying. Yes, some defensive things were buffed, but they also gave nearly all characters things that nullify those buffs. They gave near-fullscreen tracking moves, stances that close the distance almost instantly, buffing stance mix-ups, character weaknesses were being removed, buffs to frame advantage handed out like candy. I've seen clips where people were forced to block for over 10 seconds because pressing anything in that sequence would mean you lost 70% of your health bar. Yes, that was a problem in season 1, but that's why people wanted less character power. The devs would later increase the health total to 200 to combat the power-creep, and while it somewhat helped, it inadvertently made some lower damage characters weaker by proxy.  Season 3 was marketed with the line "back to basics", we were obviously excited. We thought the devs were finally listening. But those devs would later release a statement that essentially told everyone to lower their expectations, contradicting their big season 3 trailer. When the patch dropped, people quickly realized that season 3 offered more of the same, and very little else that the players wanted. A couple characters got rightfully nerfed (very slightly), but characters were buffed yet again. I realize that adding new moves make that inevitable, but in a game as volatile as this, it becomes a big problem very quickly. Some heat smashes were adjusted in some ways, but buffed in others (and they look ridiculous in-game). Animations were reused. Moves from previous iterations being toted as "new moves". The patch is more of a "season 2.5" than season 3, and people have been waiting an entire year for significant changes to the game.  All of this paints a very poor picture of the devs. The lying, the backtracking, the recycled animations, the poor balance, the empty promises. All of these combined with a near-glacial update schedule means that people are left to stew in whatever issue they have with the game. I have spent over four thousand hours on tekken 7, and i was willing to put in the time to adjust and learn tekken 8. I have not touched this game in many months and I do not intend to pick it up again unless there are drastic positive changes.

I already did not like the idea of a resource in Tekken on release. I feel like it takes away from the characters and skill expression of the player. You do nothing to earn heat and you get it every round. It is always accessible via heat burst. Simply enter heat and use your heat moves. I do not find that fun to pilot or play against. If heat is going to stay in the game you should have to earn it.        2. Heat smashes are too strong. They offer extremely high reward for little cost and risk. If a mid heat smash hits you at minimum you take 50 damage. If you block you are very minus and likely taking a 50/50 stance mix up. If you manage to step some characters will fly by you and make it difficult to punish. Wallsplatting heat smashes were in the game for an insultingly long time. My review of Tekken 8 after hitting G.O.D  Positives:  - Customization is really thought out with a lot of old costume presets that you can fully alter with different color pallets. There are more acessories to choose from that can add great detail to your outfits. New artwork for the presets that have really cool designs and coloring.  - The OST for Tekken 8 is really good with great composing and match well with the stages they're made for.  - The story mode for tekken 8 is a solid 8/10 is adds a good progession and depth to the characters and their background. The story fleshes out the drama and tension between the mishima family and the rest of the world. The most development we see is in JIn and his struggle to use his devil powers and not lose himself using them.    - The arcade mode in this game has been updated dramatically from the last installation and now has a quest mode where you play as a character you create and take on other AI opponents in a tournoment/arcade quest to become the KING OF IRON FIST.  - The training features have been fully developed into this game to allow for proper niche situation training for people that wish to enhance their skills with the game and become better tekken players. e.g. frame data, throw escape training, string punishment E.T.C  -  Stage design is really good and looks amazing. the new updated engine and textures add greatly to the design of the stages making them look fantastic.    - Character movesets are really fleshed out with new moves and a new bound system that adds large depth to a lot of character combos. All characters have great moves sets that cater to a persons playstyle if they like Stance-rushdown, Defensive, Offensive E.T.C.   Negatives  - The balancing in this game is honestly my main dislike of this game. This game has the potential to be the best fighting game out right now but its horrible balancing of characters denies this game that ability.   Firstly, Heat was a difficult mechanic to deal with at the beginning because it was new and plunged a lot of new and old tekken players into a very aggresive fight mechanic that basically made every character 100x more aggressive and threatning.   But, by season 2 the character balancing was made 1000x worse, all characters we exponentially buffed with more mix-ups, 50/50s and plus-frame moves that were not needed at all. This change to the characters ruined Defence and overall character identity because all characters had become strong in both offence and defence ruining the weaknesses of all characters.  Currently in season 3, they have made a good step forward to undo these buffs to characters by nerfing heat across the board to all characters. However, there is a lot of work that needs to be made in order for it to become a GOOD figting game   Right now as of 27/04/2026 I rate this game a 6.5/10   (p.s this rating is open to adjustment if they continue to balance this game correctly)

Do you like fighting games that punish you for trying to use your brain? Fighting games where one mistake causes your opponent to launch you into the air for a juggle so long that you have all the time in the world to go to the bathroom, come back downstairs, realise you forgot to wash your hands, go back upstairs and wash them, come back downstairs and make a cup of coffee, feed your pet, pour your drink, maybe make some toast, wait for the toaster to pop, take your toast out of the toaster and butter it, then cut it, then go back into your living room to see you're still being juggled in your opponents combo? Then boy oh boy do namco have the game for you!!!!  Tekken 8 is at times a great game. The graphics are honestly top notch which took me by surprise considering just how much i usually dislike the unreal engine look. The character roaster is respectable in its size at 32 (although for tekken standards is pretty disappointing, considering tekken 7 launched with 36, tekken 6 launched with 41, and tekken tag 2 launched with 59) and the ability to customise which songs are used for each stage, by using almost all tekken music  throughout the series is pretty cool (although minus points for removing yoshimitsu's tekken 2 ps1 theme, as well as cutting about half of the track "karma" from tekken 6, starting the song after the minute or so of amazing buildup in favour of immediately beginning with the drop)   As for the bad though, omg. Where to start. Soundtrack exclusions, and the lesser character roaster mentioned earlier are bad obviously. The main issues for me are the slow death of the series identity in favour of homogenization, and the way the gameplay is handled. Firstly, why does every game need some form of mortal kombat style x ray move? Here in tekken 8, as well as tekken 7 its called a rage art and works exactly the same. An attack that if it lands turns into a cutscene where both players just have to stand there with their thumbs up their ass's waiting to be able to play the game again. Just like street fighter theres a meter system that when activated offers different moves to the player as well as the opportunity to extend combos. Just like dead or alive there's wall breaks that allow you to knock an opponent through to get to another area of the stage (they started copying this from dead or alive in tekken 6 tbf but still). Just like mortal kombat again theres an 8 hour campaign mode that focuses on a small handful of characters, and essentially sticks its middle finger up at any character the games plot deems not important (essentially if you don't get an erection at the thought of spending almost all 8 hours just playing as jin, you're gonna be disappointed)  Then we get to the gameplay and i've never played something in my life that i've enjoyed and utterly despised as much as tekken 8. You're practically punished for trying to place any value in defence and get rewarded for just spamming the ♥♥♥♥ out of buttons like an 8 year old who's just drank red bull for the first time. The casual aspect of just picking tekken up, playing things and learning as you go honestly feels dead at this point. If you don't go immediately go into practice mode and spend a few hours learning combos, utility moves and how to punish, you may as well just refund the game. Unless you want to spend another couple hours learning those characters in practice mode so you don't get your ass handed to you online because the games levelled all these other characters up when you haven't even played as them, you may as well never play another character again. To play this game properly and importantly, have fun, you'll need to have a some things:  1. A Growth Mindset: Like any Soulsborne games, Tekken will stress your perseverance. Sometimes you'll be hit with some bullsh*t and you'd want to rage and break your controller. Get into the habit of taking accountability for your losses (you will lose a lot) instead of blaming your opponent. Cuz really, there's no teammates to place your blame on. I like playing this game because of that. It's very important that you keep your cool, and ask yourself  "what could've I done to avoid that move/situation etc."  The game's pretty technical and there's lots of niche game mechanics and strategies, so for the first 20 hours or so, you'll just be learning Tekken fundamentals on top of how to use your fighter. A lot of mistakes will be made so try to enjoy making them cuz all of your mistakes are an opportunity to learn.   Besides winning games, learning new things and applying the knowledge you worked so hard on is the most fun aspect of Tekken.  2. Fast reflexes: Every single action in the game happens in less than 1 second, or 60 frames. You'll have to learn to consistently react to moves 26 frame (400ms) moves off the rip, and anticipate anything faster than that. So I really don't recommend playing this game when you're a bit tired, unless you want to get f*cked in the ass by a King player cosplaying as John Cena. Get your 8 hours of sleep, go for a run and stretch for a bit, eat healthy, and have a cup of coffee before playing. Taking breaks from matches is also a good idea since this game is mentally draining.  3. Don't take the game seriously. That's how you have fun. There are some balancing issues and moves with this game, so try to expect that. But overall, this is the most beginner friendly Tekken game ever. I wish this game was just as popular as Street Fighter 6, but the nerds at Bamco are morons when it comes to balancing fighters.   But yeah if you don't mind losing a bunch times and you like competition then this game's pretty decent. This game is hard like Sekiro, if you've ever played it.

This new gen of Tekken is generally keeping its fundamentals down, and.. It is somewhat difficult to tell.  [i]„The better you are, the less fun the game becomes, and vice-versa.“[/i]  The character design over here is amazing. One can easily tell that they've put tonsa effort into it. Many of the previous characters are back, and although some still aren't and probably won't be comming to Tekken 8, they will feel different. And it's not just their moveset that's gonna differ, but their personality and overall reactions while fighting with them will differ.  Customization part of this game is somewhat more expanded than in the previous one, and one can easily find some neat and creative ways to impress even the opponent. Silly thinking, but many players take this to the next level and customize their characters to look like characters from other fictional genres, whether we are talking about anime, movies, mangas.. It doesn't matter. Some will make the use of it, some won't, and it is definitely possible.  Those are the neat and positive parts that made me go for it, and I don't really regret it in the end. ... However, my expectations did differ, because I experienced a next level greediness that I've never had to deal with before. No one's warning about it - Not the developers, not the playerbase.. It's a mess, and a huge trap for the newbie players. The store page is being updated with each season, too, so the present informations aren't misleading at all. It's just that there's nothing said about you not getting the future content.. Which I kind of expected to get, as most of the videogames' Ultimate Editions do come out even with its future content. Or at least have used to, back then..  [code]Buying Ultimate Edition prior to the upcoming seasons [u]won't grant you[/u] the content of the upcoming seasons. You will only receive the content of the current season and the past seasons.[/code] -> So, to those who wanna go for the Ultimate Edition to have everything unlocked.. You may need to wait for the last season to begin.. Which is gonna be at least another three years.   You might be asking, what have I had in mind with the initial statement about enjoying the game far more while being inexperienced..? Eh, exactly what it says. And that's truthful. If you've ever played other competitive videogames, do be warned in-advance that Tekken and other fighting videogames do take it to the next level. .. This videogame is the pure definition of what it means to be competitive.  Players do drill each little silly unimportant detail that's there to be found. A milisecond faster input? They must know the chart for it. And they're not satisfied until reaching this perfection.. Which is to be said somewhat admirable, but on the other hand, it becomes clear that the term fun vanishes from the videogame entirely, and pretty much forever for each player who falls into this rabbithole. Because once they learn and master the flow charts.. There's no going back. The muscle memory will keep them there, and they will remain stuck there ever since..  We're no longer talking about learning some noticeably faster inputs, but inputs that do connect to the hitboxes faster for just those tiny time frames that even human eyes can't notice and react to. Yet, people do that.. Basically, one messed up input, and your character is sent flying to the air and you can't do anything for pretty much the rest of the round, because the players have so mastered the combo inputs that it will never end and you will be midair for at least three quarters of your health bar. (This is how Tekken has always been in a nutshell, but I realized it only now and here.)  And it gets even worse, particularly with how you're gonna be approached as a new player, but that's something I won't expand on any further here. Let's just say that the gatekeeping level here is extreme, on par with some other communities out there.   So, what's fun in this game, you might be asking?  - Perfectly laying down the inputs for your character. This probably feels satisfying..? I wouldn't know, but it feels like button mashing and I don't enjoy such interactions. I wanna know what'd my opponents do, not to limit the interactions between me and them by perfecting the combos and leaving them midair for the whole round. - New stories. Yeah! For those who are here for the singleplayer part of the game, you're being covered! The game does expand on the Mishima story as from the previous title, as well as offers some more character development for its past characters. And that's not all.. To help you handle the basics, provides another singleplayer game mode that lets you interact with the game at more or less your own pace. Arcade game mode is there aswell, but that's different. The known and popular Treassure Battle is gone though. - Coming up with your own and personal customization ideas for your favorite characters. I wouldn't have expected myself to say it, but this has played a huge part for me. I've spent countless of hours customizing my characters, and that's always changing with new stuff from the battlepasses and such.  So, I think this does about cover it all. Whether I'd recommend this game or not, though..?  If you are.. - Casual player? Only if you genuinely care about the story and character development. There's nothing else for you here, because the multiplayer part will push you away. - Semi-casual / Semi-competitive player? Maaaybe, the game's got a lot in the store for ya, but it's by no means gonna hold you here and with a positive attitude. It will be an uphill battle with ups and downs. - Competitive player? This is the game for you. This is the game for grinding each little detail and knowing how everything works, how each little detail changes everything, not just the bigger picture, but even the small picture at its core.  Whether I'd personally recommend it ..? That's the neat part. I don't know.. It's a mixed conclusion, but because singleplayer elements are limiting and do only last for so long.. I will go with a negative one here.  Yup, that's all. Do have fun!

First off, I recently moved to steam and originally had 1000+ hours on Tekken 8 on PS5.  Initially upon the game's release, it was clear that game is extremely unbalanced and in an unhealthy state, but most players were still learning the game so no one was able to truly show how broken this game was. Balance patch after balance patch, the game started improving. Abusive and braindead mechanics were being toned down, slowly. Then comes season 2, where they doubled down x10 on the very same mechanics everyone hated, making the game even worse than it's release state. Not only that, but they were also extremely slow in making in balance readjustments.  Many players, such as I, had left the game at the first month of season. It's been around a year now and with the season 3 announcement, I decided to give this game a chance again with a clear mind. While the balancing remains abysmal, there is countless amount of fun to be had with friends, as long as you don't take this game seriously competition-wise. It has beautiful graphics, big selection of characters, and still the Tekken identity we all have come to love.  If you want to play this game offline alone, or online competitively, then I would not recommend this game for you at all. But if you find it on sale and want to brawl it out with the bros for fun, absolutely buy it, you will have a blast.

Probably the two things I wish was different about this game the most are 1) a stronger defensive system and 2) improved single player modes. SF6 World Tour mode is my favorite single player content in a fighting game ever, and I want all fighting games to incorporate a similar mode, but don't just copy it, improve upon it and innovate because it's still just a starting point. As far as the defensive system goes. It seems like there is a current focus on casuals and accessibility. How about making defense more accessible to newcomers, like ducking and sidestepping. Right now ducking and sidestepping feels so risky.  It would be cool if there was a single player mode where it teaches you how to Korean back dash and you get rewards for completing it. Also don't we want to encourage people to practice? I wish i got battle pass points for spending time in training mode, not just ranked.

Tekken 8 takes many of the most controversial elements from Tekken 7 and amplifies them. If you’re a long-time Tekken player who values spacing, punishment, and disciplined neutral, this entry may feel like a step in the wrong direction.  The biggest issue right now is how much the game feels like a lottery system. The reward-to-risk ratio is heavily skewed. Some characters can dish out massive damage — sometimes triple what others can — with far less execution required. Between one-button combo routes, Heat activations, and Rage Arts, it’s entirely possible to outplay your opponent for most of the round and still lose to a single sequence that requires significantly less effort.  Heat was clearly designed to encourage aggression, but in practice it often turns matches into momentum swings that feel disproportionate. Instead of careful advantage-building, rounds frequently come down to who converts first into an optimized damage sequence.  The juggling is also excessive. Tekken has always had launchers and air combos, but Tekken 8 pushes this to an extreme. A single launch can lead into wall carry, wall splat, stage interaction, and further extensions — sometimes sending you back into the air again. Matches often turn into long, non-interactive sequences where one player is essentially watching their character get carried across the screen.  Long combos aren’t inherently bad, but when they dominate the match flow, the sense of interaction suffers.  If you enjoy explosive, high-damage, aggression-heavy fighting games, you may find Tekken 8 exciting. But if you prefer traditional Tekken fundamentals — movement, spacing, consistent execution, and measured risk — this entry may feel frustrating.  As it stands, I cannot recommend this game to traditional Tekken fans.

It does have it's drawbacks competitively as I feel the heat system needs greater balance; that combined with the rage art upon getting totally demolished gives those on the wrong end of a beat down a magical ability to unfairly comeback with one button. It's not earned, no skill attached, just given as a "get of jail free card" rewarding bad play.   Characters like King benefit from that, with their strongest moves connected to comeback mechanics so players will often just wait for those to kick in and try get a cheap win as opposed to actually learning the game and fighting. It results in very dull, uninspired, monotonous, repetitive, copy and paste gameplay from a lot of the player base.  The netcode has also deteriorated since launch, with the connection showing not actually being the connection present when facing opponents online, allowing people with terrible internet connections to ruin sets.  There is still a lot of fun to be had here with a great story element and a lot of modes and customisation options to really diversify your experience. Those issues I mentioned just need to be dealt with for it to return to it's former glory and go beyond. The Potential is there for sure.

...I really wanted to like Tekken 8.  I started playing Tekken when Tekken 3 launched on PS1. I quite literally grew up playing Tekken as it was my favorite fighting game. Heck, I even have a tattoo of Jin's tattoo. I have games, movies, soundtracks, posters/wall scrolls, figures and even 1/4 scales statues of Jin and Devil Jin. Over 20 years of being a fan of Tekken (primarily a Jin player) and despite REALLY wanting to like Tekken 8...I don't. I obtained the platinum trophy so I put time into the game however even as a Tekken fanboy I don't think I can recommend this one.  "The Good" (single player content): If you are not into competitive play to test your skills online then this game is solid. You have a story mode, you have arcade quest (non tekken lore story about being an arcade player), you have an arcade mode, etc. There is single player content available in the game. There is a, serviceable, character customization mode. Not as good as previous games in my opinion however passable. Phenomenal soundtrack, there is some great music that I absolutely love hearing when it pops up randomly in my playlist while out and about or training.   My main problem with Tekken 8 is...the combat.  I know Tekken has been catering to the e-sports crowd with the latest entries however there was this delicate balance of "substance" and "flash" where at it's core Tekken was a fighting game that prioritized proper spacing, proper timing, etc. aka substance over "I want cool stuff to look cool" aka flash. My main issue with Tekken 8's combat is that I do not feel like I am in "control" of MY character. What do I mean? Successfully hitting certain attacks will cause this unskippable animation of you knocking the opponent away then running after them to reengage in a forced mandatory 50/50. Yes the first time it looks cool and it doesn't last too long however...after many matches those few seconds become minutes/hours of watching the same animation. Unfortunately the animation is tied to a common attack I use with Jin and I legit find myself avoiding using the attack because I do not want to initiate the animation. I, the player, just want to knock the opponent on the ground however Tekken 8 decides to turn it into a Dragonball pursuit attack by default. I am not a fan of the heat system (basically certain attacks put you into this mode where you do chip damage to blocking opponents and I think heal a small amount of health of recoverable for attacking?) I did my best to ignore the system. I know historically Tekken has had "chip damage" via the supercharge however the drawback of supercharging was how long the animation took and how vulnerable you are while supercharged because you CANNOT block and your opponent's attack counted as a "counter hit" so there was this whole risk/reward tied to it. With this heat system I didn't really see the downside of using it? So I'd imagine heat moves are just spammed online similar to how people spammed those hyper armor attacks in Tekken Revolution. Tekken has been my favorite fighting game because of the "freedom" you have in combat however whether it was in story mode, arcade mode and the few matches I played online I had to deal with "I correctly predicted opponent's next attack, I threw an counter attack that connected on the opponent...however due to the special properties of the opponent's attack instead of knocking down and/or preventing the attack the opponent has hyper armor, opponent attacks through my attack and combos" You can have proper spacing and timing however because you did not use the "specific attack" with the "specific properties" you are punished because Tekken 8 says so. So what am I supposed to do? Prioritize using the specific attacks with specific properties while ignoring the rest of the command list? Buy it on sale—Great gameplay, but questionable balancing & DLC.  Despite the recent doom-and-gloom in the community and the news about the series lead Harada leaving, I actually like the core of the game.  It doesn’t feel exactly like Tekken 7 mechanically; it’s much more accessible. If you’re a newer player or just want to jump in and have fun, the "Special Style" (combo-assist) makes it much easier to play without memorizing 100-hit strings. The dynamics are solid and it feels better to play than Street Fighter 6 in my opinion—it just offers a welcome variety that SF6 lacks right now.  However, there are some glaring issues you should know before buying:  The Roster Paywall: It feels like they locked "given" characters (classic fighters that should be base roster) behind a paywall just to sell passes.  Lack of Stages: The base game really needs more stages. You'll get tired of the current rotation pretty quickly.  Pay-to-Win Balancing: This is my biggest gripe. The balancing is off. Some of the DLC characters are way too OP—Clive, in particular, is a nightmare to fight against. He has moves that feel practically unblockable and he hits like a truck. The game desperately needs a balance patch to fix these DLC power spikes.  Fluff: I didn't care for the Arcade Quest/Avatar customization at all; it feels like filler. The soundtrack is also just "okay"—it sounds almost the same as previous entries.  Verdict: If you can grab the base game for under $30, it’s worth it. Don't buy the expensive editions or the Season Pass upfront. Just get the base game and maybe buy the one or two specific characters you’ll actually use. You can add the rest later if they ever fix the balancing.

When it comes to fighting games, monetization grows more and more egregious year by year. I think we all know this; Dead or Alive, Street Fighter, and now Tekken all sport disgustingly priced season passes and other cut out knick knacks for DLC. I think I remember frame data being sold for one of them too now. As much as I hate it, this review is not about the publisher's disgusting greed, it's about the game itself.   Tekken 8 is the most fun I've had with a Tekken title since Tekken 4 in the early 2000s when I was a kid. Tekken 7 felt too clunky for me and perhaps, it was a lack of technical skill that made that game hard to play. But 8 feels so vital and fresh to play that it is astounding. The gameplay is weighty but never cumbersome. The focus on aggression is right up my alley as I play that way in my favorite fighting game Dead or Alive. As much as it pains me to say it, this tears DOA up in content and enjoyment. I have not played a fighting game with this much joy in some time. I love the Ghost system to practice and become more refined instead of button mashing. I have a terrible memory for combos but practicing the inner workings of the game never felt easier.   There are a few caveats to my praise. The Heat system and Rage Arts sometimes feel like get out of jail free cards and can be abusable. Of course, these attacks can be avoided but I feel cheap using them at times. I can't speak on the more technical things like movesets and balancing but I haven't felt anything "off" on that front but then again, I don't own most of the DLC characters that I hear are broken.  All in all, aside from the monetization, this is a very enjoyable title. Avoid the passes, only get the characters you really want, and keep it pushing - definitely worth it on sale.

While Tekken 8 still is fun at times cause to its core it still feels and plays like Tekken, its a former shell of itself in comparison to the overall tone, direction, and gameplay. To elaborate the previous Tekken games focused on their characters using real life martial arts as being the foundation/forefront of the series.  What really holds Tekken 8 back for me is how far it has drifted from the grounded identity that made the older entries feel so captivating. Earlier Tekken games took themselves more seriously in both presentation and tone. The cutscenes, while sometimes over-the-top, still felt deliberate and restrained, giving weight to the characters and their martial arts backgrounds. Fighters were clearly rooted in real-world disciplines first, with supernatural elements used sparingly to enhance the story rather than dominate it. In contrast, Tekken 8 leans heavily into spectacle at the expense of that balance, often feeling more like a constant sensory overload than a disciplined fighting game. Gameplay wise, the shift toward hyper-aggression makes it increasingly difficult to play solid defense without being punished severely. Matches often feel decided by momentum rather than decision-making, where a single mistake can result in losing over half your health to a long, unskippable juggle combo that doubles as a cutscene. Defensive fundamentals feel less rewarding, and neutral play takes a back seat to nonstop pressure. While this design may appeal to newer or more casual audiences, it strips away much of the strategic depth and tension that made earlier Tekken games so engaging and satisfying to master.  Transition into business decisions & monetization: On top of these gameplay and stylistic changes, Tekken 8’s business decisions further dampen the experience. The reuse of DLC characters from the previous game raises the question of why players are expected to pay again for fighters they already purchased once before(same DLC characters as T7 for those who havent played). Making Heihachi—one of the most iconic and long-standing staples of the franchise—paid DLC feels especially tone-deaf. Add in microtransactions for in-game currency and the reselling of old costumes from previous Tekken titles, and it begins to feel less like fan service and more like double-dipping. These choices don’t ruin the game outright, but they do leave a sour aftertaste that contrasts sharply with how much care and respect the series once showed its legacy.  Final Verdict 6/10 Overall the game is far from bad just unfortunate that leaned so hard to catering to new players. more game modes would be nice. 1 rage art per match sounds more ideal to me making your special feel more akin to a final resort like attack. Probably a unpopular opinion but low parries should be buffed if they're so stuck on this game aggressive fighting direction. Feels more like Tekken x Soul Caliber 8 now especially considering the new character coming out.  Hopefully they earned enough in sales and microtransactions to give a OG tekken player what I want, A Tekken Legacy Collection bundle on steam(yea never gonna happen but a man can dream)

Tekken 8 closes in on its second year, so I figured I might give my take on the game these past two years:  The game in its core is fun, it still feels like Tekken. Main difference is that compared to past titles, the game heavily favors aggressive gameplay, which simplifies the gameplan of each match. On paper, this does not pose as a problem, until looking into it all in more detail. The defensive player is given few options to play against the aggressive playstyle, making them feel overwhelmed by the amount of offense coming at them. Season 1 started out like this and then got balanced out fairly evenly, while Season 2 doubled down on the aggressive style of gameplay by removing the blatant weaknesses of each character. While this too got balanced out over time, it created immense distrust for the players, where many left the game in protest.  I can personally say that I still enjoy the game for what it is, since it still feels like Tekken to me. While a bit reluctant, I do still recommend people to play this game, especially if they have not played past Tekken titles. Hopefully, season 3 will launch on a positive note, bringing both new and old players.

Season 2 absolutely ruined this game... Before Season 2 I would've recommended it proudly. It had some kinks to work out, but it should've been manageable. Season 2 did the exact opposite of what everyone asked for...   It's a perfect storm of incompetent devs, greedy execs and a lack of proper direction, that killed everything Tekken was about. When even the pros are losing their ♥♥♥♥ with how terribly designed the game is, you know you done ♥♥♥♥♥♥ it up! And now that Harada is leaving, there's absolutely ZERO hope for this to ever be fixed. He was arguably not in much control anyway, so I guess it's just going to get worse now that he's not there at all.  First of all... What's good about the game? This is the most stylish Tekken has ever been... Fancy graphics, cool outfits and customization, the music is really good too and the updated animations are just chef's kiss... Also, hitting your opponent has never felt more satisfying than this. The sound direction (excluding voice acting) is amazing. And if you're a combo artist, you're gonna love the overcomplicated combo system and the crazy stuff you can do with it, especially with the new Heat system. The practice mode is also one of the most elaborated and helpful systems I've seen on any fighting game (with one caveat in the bad section). But that's about it... If it were S1, there'd be more, but sadly that's not the case...  Onto the bad: The game is riddled with so many issues, I have to section them off. I'll try to be short and to the point with each:  Sidestepping: Doesn't work. You WILL get clipped 90% of the time and this seems to be by design, because they amped up the tracking in S2 after "buffing" sidestepping. That should tell you what mindset these devs are on...  Hitboxes: Inconsistent as hell... You will get hit from a back turned opponent, whiffing attacks will randomly connect and sometimes you can literally catch your character's fist go through the heart of your opponent sticking out the other side and still not connect. On top of that, nearly every character has been given a ton of evasive moves, that randomly duck under highs and jump over lows, sometimes even mids are skipped... This is one of the main factors leading into the next issue:  Fundamentals: Tekken 8 prides itself in giving every character so many options to skip the fundamentals of Tekken, that it stops being Tekken... The evasive moves allow anyone to steal their turn back with little thought. Specialty moves like Yoshi's flash, Xiaoyu's AOP stance and lots and lots of power crush moves allow most characters to steal their turn back and skip neutral. So many moves are overtuned, that you hardly even need to use the moveset. And for most of these, the counter is often a hard read or just playing like a turtle...  Inputs: Generally the inputs feel ok. But every now and then, this game decides not to register some moves or completely misfire, often killing you in turn. Like for example ducking inputs randomly not registering. I've seen other people complain about this and I know it's not controller related, because I've gone through 4 of them and a keyboard and all exhibit the same issues.  Overall Character Design: By this I mean gameplay design. Most characters had their weaknesses removed in S2 and are now easy Jack of all Trades characters. Character identity is a thing of the past... Lots of interesting interactions and mixups were removed, lots of characters became harder focussed on stance rushdown type gameplay and overall, it just doesn't feel like the characters stand out from each other as they did pre S2.   50/50 Casino Gameplay: Most characters have had legacy moves altered or new moves introduced, that make this game more of a guessing game than a fighting game. Almost every character has stances that force a 50/50 you can't react to based on character knowledge... It's just awful, because there's no depth to it like there was before.  Combo System: Tekken 8's combo system is an absolute abomination... It's the result if adding more and more layers to extend the combos, without considering what happens on the receiving end. To simplify: You launch an opponent, perform a couple moves to juggle, sprinkle in some tailspins, usually follow up with a combo extension (in this case the Tornado, it's easy to pick up too), then perform a couple more hits, before engaging heat to resplat them on the ground, carry them to the wall and end with a wall combo, which may or may not engage a stage gimmick and resplat the opponent for a couple more hits (be it on the ground, wall or through an explosion). All that, while the receiving end gets nothing to do but watch their healthbar get deleted, usually 50% or more... Not every combo is like this obviously, but once you get to higher ranks you usually spend half the round just waiting to be able to do anything again... It's a very frustrating system, that could be easily fixed by giving the receiving player something to do to break / reduce combo damage or just by reducing the amount of combo extensions there are...
