TEKKEN 8 - A good game ruined by a lack of balancing and pay-to-win, and so much more.  Tekken 8 is a game with great visual effects, composed of new and returning characters, some of them more iconic than others. It is a game where you can enjoy the story mode, the goofy moments (fighting an army of armed soldiers with King—need I say more?), and playing with friends regardless if your friends own the game or not.  It serves as a good local multiplayer or online if you use remote play or tools like Parsec, whatever fits your taste.  You'll be golden if you play this game casually, but if you are one of those people who want to take the experience a step further and hop onto ranked matches, the nightmare begins.  I say this because Tekken 8 requires you to dedicate a good portion of your leisure time to get to an average level of expertise. Things like side-stepping, side-walking, neutral game, blocking, combos, opening up your opponent's defense, power crush usage, punishments, grab-breaks, turn awareness, and so on. Whenever you hit the current average ranks, which currently in season 2 are blue ranks, you'll have a huge necessity of labbing characters if you haven't done so already. Essentially what this means is you'll need to hop on the practice mode and start learning when to sidestep strings, moves that track to one side or the other, and when to duck and punish your opponent properly with every character in the game.   WHERE THE PROBLEMS START... Pay-to-win philosophy is quite present in this game, because if you want to have a chance against DLC characters, you have two solutions: either pay up and lab/learn the character, which means -8€ on your wallet for a character you don't even want in the first place, or you randomly find them in quick matches and take loss after loss until you eventually get the hang of them, and even then those who properly learn it in practice mode will still be better off than you. This bothers me and many others because in ranked, each loss will cost you time and effort to build back up again, and if you are unfortunate enough to so much as find a DLC character on the other side, you will lose ranked points, so your only out is to either pay and lab or get taxed in ranked points by a DLC character user.  FLAWED BALANCING I'm not the first and certainly not the last to say it, but this game is not in favor of those who want to enjoy a few ranked matches in their free time. This game features heavily and effectively broken characters like Anna Williams, Nina Williams, Hwoarang, Yoshimitsu, Bryan Fury, Jack-8, and so on. In theory, each character in this game has something that makes them flawed when it comes to balancing, be it string jailing, unpunishable lows with heavy mix-up options that make you gamble your HP bar each time those come out (Hworang mains will know what I am talking about), strings that track even when side walked (heavy position re-adjusting on Bryan's strings is an example), heat smashes with wall splats (Jin Kazama), heavy tracking, priority stealing (Yoshi's flash "parry" is as much of a threat as a rage art, basically working as a turn steal at a button's notice, so you must play around that whenever it is your turn), and the list goes on so be prepared to not have fair odds against every match up you face. HEAT BAR... In my opinion, it should not be a thing. A mechanic which changes how your character works, sometimes more or sometimes less than others depending on who you main, and that poses a threat for your opponent whenever it is activated since you can heat smash at any time and respond to most moves the other makes.  That being said, if it is meant to stay, make it so it goes down in the middle of a combo instead of it stopping or, in some cases, even regenerating it for some unknown design choice for certain characters.  CONCLUSION and TLDR If you like the game, play it. If you get enjoyment from it, keep at it. But if your red flags include modern Tekken, poor balancing or long waits for fixes, praying for your character NOT to be buffed, pay-to-win / save time, rage-inducing (for some), and a long and arduous journey to become actually good at the game essentially requiring you to only pay attention to this game to learn it from top to bottom, do not go for this game. Play something else, enjoy it, and make sure your free time is used for things worth your time and that are FUN, especially FUN and ENJOYABLE, not a competitive game with this many issues.

Namco has truly excelled with Tekken 8, featuring 32 characters at launch, including both legacy favorites and newcomers like Reina, Victor, and the coffee-loving Azucena. The game boasts a memorable soundtrack that includes the entire series library, allowing players to customize their own stage tracks. With a steady online experience, fighter customization options, and a story mode, there’s a lot to enjoy. Most fighting games should take notes on how to deliver a solid $70 package.  In terms of gameplay, Tekken 8 is the most aggressive of its predecessors. It introduces a new mechanic called "heat," which enhances fighters’ offensive capabilities with an expanded moveset, quicker recovery, and chip damage on block—perfect for making comebacks when health is low. At first, I was unsure about this concept, but once I learned how to utilize it, I grew to appreciate the heat mechanic and the direction Tekken is taking.  I particularly love the addition of Arcade Quest, a personal story mode that not only teaches new players the mechanics but also provides a glimpse of what to expect when competing online. It’s a great introduction for those who aren't ready to play online yet.  The story mode is decent; while not groundbreaking, it serves well enough to pass the time and showcases the developments in each character’s legacy.  Tekken has also introduced a fight pass, which is a timely addition. Players can enjoy grinding for artwork, cosmetics, and more if they choose to, all at an affordable price of $10, with rewards given upon completion.  One disappointment I have regarding Tekken 8 is the DLC roster. It’s frustrating that legacy characters need to be repurchased, and some guest characters leave much to be desired. For instance, where's Tifa Lockhart? A character like her, being a boxer, would fit perfectly within Tekken's roster of martial artists. Instead, we get Clive, who seems more suitable for Soul Calibur—this is quite confusing, Namco.  Tekken 8 might not be the definitive title for every veteran player, especially with its new comeback system, but it’s still a lot of fun to play with family and friends from time to time. I would rate this fighting gem a 9/10.  But seriously, Namco, where's Tifa Lockhart?

This means understanding that a character who's move looks slower than yours actually isn't because of "start-up frames" and other factors that you need to know otherwise you will likely get launched where you can sit and watch yourself get hit in a juggle combo for the next 10s. If you are really lucky you won't get splatted against the wall and might get a chance to retaliate.  It's a twitchy spam and juggle fest, which is exactly what has turned me off modern fighting games.  But again, this is an angry old man shaking his fist about things changing, so only take my advice if that applies to you.

Tekken 8 had all the hype in the world, but the final product feels like a step backward wrapped in pretty graphics. Yes, the visuals are impressive, but once you’re actually playing, the problems start piling up fast.  The new Heat system feels more like a gimmick than an evolution of the gameplay. Instead of adding depth, it pushes the game toward aggressive, brain-off rushdown that removes a lot of the strategic spacing and mind games the series is known for. Matches feel chaotic—not in a fun way, but in a sloppy, unbalanced way.  The story mode is a mess. It’s filled with cheesy dialogue, uneven pacing, and fights that feel more like interruptions than actual gameplay. Character episodes are short and forgettable, and several fan-favorite fighters feel like they were included at the last minute with almost no meaningful development.  Online play is another disappointment. Despite promises of rock-solid rollback, matchmaking is slow, unstable, and inconsistent. You either wait forever for a match or get thrown into a laggy one that ruins any sense of competition.  And don’t even get me started on the customization system. It’s shallow, limited, and somehow manages to look worse than past games that were nearly a decade old.  Overall, Tekken 8 looks good from a distance, but the moment you pick up the controller, the cracks show. Flashy graphics can’t save a fighting game that forgets what made the series great in the first place. Not worth full price.

Tekken 8 could’ve been an amazing experience, but the playerbase drags it straight into the dirt. The game pretends to be welcoming to newcomers, but the moment you hit online you’re just fed to players spamming the same meta-perfect, lab-grown combos that lock you in place for half the round. There’s no chance to learn, no room to breathe, and definitely no “fun” when every match turns into a stun-lock highlight reel for someone who’s been grinding the optimal routes for months. It’s not even about skill—it's about how the community leans obsessively into whatever the most broken, efficient combo of the week is. Instead of matches feeling like fights, they feel like cutscenes you’re forced to watch while your health bar evaporates. For a game that markets itself on excitement and accessibility, Tekken 8 ends up feeling like a gated club where newer players exist only to get farmed. Honestly, the whole experience gets old fast.

I haven't really played Tekken since Tekken 2 and 3 so my knowledge of the game is limited to those titles, so this review will be from that perspective, my friends who I played with also had not touched Tekken since 4 or 5, mostly playing locally.  Tekken 8 is a lot different than the earlier games, it is nostalgic seeing old characters* but they have changed visually, it is still great to see them again though in new and revived forms; and this game is visually impressive and runs well enough.   The gameplay is different in that it's not all about memorising moves and spacing, since now they have an easy mode that you can press that spams out moves and combos for you, again we all agreed not to use this, new players will bear the brunt of and with this feaure though.  There is also now heat and heat smashes, basically a limited resource per round that lets you do extra moves, more damage, or press a button that uses up all heat but performs an instant combo deleting a portion of the opponents health if it lands, again, not something we were proud of using but you get to smirk at them when it lands.  The least proud button that we didn't want to put people through (Or at least the animations are quite novel and cool to watch the first time around) is something called Rage, basically if you are low health you can press "the funny button", if this single strike hit lands the opponent has to watch as you perform a 20 second long cutscene that will remove over half of their health. Usually these don't land but if they do, boy they are going to *love* you so much.  *Ah yes, the asterix, under characters...Yes charging players money for characters that are classically base game characters, they themselves being replaced mostly by characters that bore me or I haven't heard of, a lot of the roster was hit or miss for me but this is personal preference, there are definitely some new favourites of mine in tekken 8.   This game is heavy on the Item store, it will pop up every time you launch the game begging you to interact with the store, dlc and economy, in fact they released heihachi (An absolute Tekken staple) as DLC even though cannonically he was killed or something? That's fine, maybe? They advertised him in a youtube video which came with a cool map, whatever. Oh, god, the price...  ...Except you pay seperately for the map...Then you also pay for the character, they advertised them together so as to seem they are related, how, neat? This goes on and on. It's greedy. Traditionally core characters should not be DLC in my opinion, or they should not release for this title at all. But that's not my decision.  I tried multiplayer for a bit, you know I work, I do other things. Apparently these people who I play against don't so I didn't bother playing against them that much. With that said there are other things you can do offline in Tekken so I applaud that, although the Singleplayer campaign is basically "I hope you're a Jin main!".  Overall solid 6/10. A little over or on the fence, beautiful looking game but you feel dirty owning it or playing it. Obviously you can read up on other people's issues with this product but to me I felt a bit bad spending €60 on this only for my favourite character to get announced back then as DLC.  tldr: im too old for this

TL;DR- Good outweighs the bad. Lots of great features and fun to be had if you put aside the small amount of issues. Heat system is a load of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and ruins a lot of matches.  I decided to update my review, as I have learned a lot since I originally posted it. Right off the bat, I just want to say it is painfully clear that the reason for most of the negative reviews is, "It's not Tekken 7." Ok, so go play Tekken 7, it's right there.  With that out of the way, I want to address the actual issues I have with the game, the biggest of which isn't a problem with the game itself- it's the monetization. There is no reason why a game that costs $60 should have paid DLC characters, with the exception of crossovers; and crossover characters should absolutely NOT be stronger than originals (*cough*Clyde*cough*). I got the game at an 85% discount, but this is a valid excuse for a negative review. The second issue I have is with how weak defense feels in relation to damage output. It feels like characters do way too much damage across the board. It's not a case of "if everyone is OP, nobody is." It's genuinely boring, because the matches feel rushed. I don't feel accomplished pressing one button to initiate a heat chain, just to follow it up with a combo that ends the round. It's not even annoying when it happens to me- it's just a really stupid mechanic. The craziest part is, I started playing AFTER they increased the max HP to 200. They need to either nerf damage across the board, or get rid of Heat chains.  Despite that major gripe I have, the good outweighs the bad. For starters, the graphics are absolutely stunning, especially for this genre. The amount of detail in the character models and environment are genuinely beautiful, and it adds a special level of immersion. Next thing I really like is the Rage Art mechanic. It can completely change the outcome of a match, and it adds a level of strategy to both offense and defense that is genuinely exciting. The Ghost Battle features are incredible. Wanna practice against that guy that just destroyed you in a set? Download his ghost data and go to town. Wanna fight YOURSELF? Pick one of your own ghosts and smash your monitor after you lose to yourself. The AI learning is really f*cking cool, and it will help you improve. The replay system is another strong-suit. Can't figure out why you lost that match? Watch the replay and the game will pause it and tell you what you could have done differently at any given moment. I could keep going on and on about features like this, from learning combos, to a full blown story mode, the offline content is plentiful AND worthwhile. Online is obviously why most people are going to buy it. The rollback netcode is great, the ranked grind is fun, and the Fight Lounge is actually really cool, and a great place to socialize in a PlayStation Home kinda way. Also, boobs. Can't forget about boobs.

Tekken 8 is a competitive 3D fighting game that advances the long-running series with refined mechanics, aggressive pacing, and a strong focus on character individuality. Built on Unreal Engine 5, it delivers high visual fidelity and fluid animations that enhance both readability and impact during matches. The game maintains Tekken’s core movement system while introducing new features designed to make offense more rewarding and dynamic.  The narrative continues the Mishima family conflict, centering on Jin Kazama’s confrontation with Kazuya. The story mode blends cinematic sequences with playable segments, emphasizing dramatic stakes and character motivations. While the plot follows familiar themes of power, legacy, and revenge, its presentation benefits from improved visuals and more cohesive mission structure.  Combat remains deeply technical but leans further toward forward pressure. The Heat system is the centerpiece, granting characters temporary offensive boosts that expand combo routes, extend pressure, and enable new strategic layers. Rage Arts return as cinematic finishers, giving matches dramatic closing moments. Movement precision, punishment knowledge, and matchup awareness remain essential to high-level play.  The roster showcases a mix of returning favorites and newcomers, each with unique mechanics, stances, or signature techniques. Characters feel distinct without losing cohesiveness within the core system. Updates to move lists and animations improve clarity, allowing players to better recognize threats and react during fast exchanges. Customization options expand visual variety without affecting balance.  Online functionality features rollback netcode and a lobby system designed for smooth matchmaking. Ranked, quick match, and group play modes support competitive engagement, while training tools offer detailed frame data, scenario recording, and character guides. These resources make the game more approachable for new players without diluting its competitive depth.  Presentation is a major highlight. Detailed character models, dynamic stages, and impactful hit effects contribute to a more visceral sense of combat. The soundtrack blends electronic, rock, and thematic stage tracks to match the intensity of matches and narrative tone. Visual clarity during high-speed sequences helps maintain focus despite the increased aggression of the new mechanics.  Tekken 8 succeeds by modernizing the series with an offense-oriented system, robust online features, and high production values. It preserves the strategic complexity that defines Tekken while offering tools and mechanics that encourage more active play. For veterans and newcomers seeking a refined, high-intensity 3D fighter, it stands as one of the most polished entries in the franchise.

A very good TEKKEN game with some major flaws that let it down.  One of the major flaws being that the game is way too offensive now. Playing it smart and safe is dis-encouraged, and sometimes you are forced into unwinnable or near-impossible 50/50s purely due to pressure and the fact that you usually have to do some sort of maneuver to get out of the situation, leaving you vulnerable.  Even worse is the disgustingly advantageous Special Styles. While I understand that, in higher ranks, this is quite counterable and not much of an issue (if it gets used at all), it can really unbalance the lower ranks and lower the skill gaps meaning a beginner with Special Style and a decent idea of the game's mechanics has an advantage over someone who prefers not to use it. This would be all right as an optional feature - but it is allowed in RANKED, with no option to filter it out!  The heat system is MEH, I wouldn't care if it was removed altogether but I haven't ever found it game-breaking or grossly unbalanced. I especially like the risk/reward factor that the Rage Arts bring to the game. And they are great to look at, although they can drag on sometimes.  I feel this is why this game has become controversial amongst TEKKEN fans, mostly the competitive high-rank players. But I don't think this is so much the case for more casual or semi-serious players. The game offers plenty of Online and Offline content and doesn't feel unfinished.  What the game partially lacks in substance it makes up for in style. TEKKEN 8 is by far the best looking TEKKEN game I have ever played. The character models look outstanding, the stages are gorgeous, and the amount of detail in ever corner of the game graphically is impressive. The visual effects during fights are maybe a little overdone, but it definitely looks flashy, and it feels responsive.  I would recommend this game GENERALLY but there are some very major flaws that need to be ironed out. I can definitely understand people's point of view with the glaring issues in the game. If you are buying purely for story content and offline modes, there is a lot to be enjoyed. If you are a ranked player who is fairly competitive and high rank, and you are coming from a previous TEKKEN, do not set your expectations too high.

Picked up Tekken 8 just the funny customization options, stayed because of Clive, dropped it because of how bad it feels to play. They toned down defensive play to force more aggressive matches, but in doing so almost punishes trying to be aggressive while keeping a decent defense. Hitboxes/hurtboxes that are either way too large than they need to be, moves tracking people on whiff, absolutely insane interactions with not just the stage(s), but also the camera, a whole season of no real changes/fixes/balancing for the sake of tournament events when the game badly needs it...   So much feels sacrificed for the beginner Tekken player experience, but being said beginner player (I have under 40 hours in Tekken 7 and one (1) in Tekken Tag 2) and playing more/getting better, it just feels awful to play. The "hehe funny 50/50 gamble" stops being funny when you're forced into coin-tosses every match, where losing the toss results in a combo that lasts so long you may as well be watching a cutscene. Characters with parries (shout-out my goat Clive) can parry some things, but other things break it, and it feels downright arbitrary as to why. Ditto to armored moves: some armored moves just break others for no reason other than "because why not". Getting hit by moves that are nowhere near you because the hitboxes in this game are absolutely massive for no reason other than... what, to make spectating more interesting? To make rounds end faster? Get a grip.  It's a fun game if you just run private matches with friends, and the character customization ([i]when it isn't locked behind a paywall[/i]) is neat (unless you play Kuma or Panda, in which case I'm so sorry), but other than that? Tekken 8 just feels like all style, no substance.

At this point, I honestly believe, they are making these changes on purpose to push out legacy players. They don't want players like knee, Arslan and other top players dictating the game. They want legacy players in general, gone.  So, I actually liked this game on release. S1 was really fun and the devs, were making changes in the right direction. Then for S2 it went the complete opposite direction (or how they intended the game to be on release) and they basically nuked the game. [/b]  [h2] General overview [/h2]  [*] If you're new to Tekken, you'll probably have fun regardless. Just press buttons, experiment and enjoy.  [*]Get this out the way first - in game store with in game currency (tekken coins) that you purchase with real money. Now I don't mind cosmetic packs being sold, except the PUBLISHERS (Bamco) have this unethical way of selling cosmetic items. The new stuff made for T8 look nice, the older ported stuff look off, lazy. The way it's sold is predatory; first it's handled outside of Steam, what happens if servers go down, like what is this transaction tied to? Second, packs are sold separately (male/female). Third, the amount of Tekken coins purchased, with how much stuff cost, encourages you to buy more coins, you always have coins left over,  from purchases, you can't just buy two things, you will need to buy more coins, with again coins left over and repeat the cycle.   [*]Story - average, cliche, anime story, with some hype moments and video graphic cut scenes that look nice. But, why a mass genocide murderer is forgiven?...Because he believes in his heart! It is peak anime story telling.  [*]Graphics/art style - Easily the best looking Tekken game, with nice looking effects (but too much). Art style is weird, as there is a global war going on and some characters look dress for the part (Law, Paul, Jack 8 ect) and the rest look normal, clean aesthetic; same with the stages, only one stage, where you're fighting in an broken building of a warzone, seems to match the games tone of an all out war going on. [*]Music - I really like the tracks/ost in T8 and the final round track versions get hype! Just like T7, Tekken jukebox is great, being able to customise the music is nice.  [*]Gameplay - it's bad, just terrible.  The game has no options to counter (or any counter play options) as the defender; due to the nerfed movement, you can't back dash out of block strings, you are literally locked down into guessing mix-ups or create any meaningful space between you and your opponent, because there is no neutral in this game, characters are able to skip the neutral game with moves that travel from range 4 to 1 (basically halfway across screen). They made back dash easier for new people, which was a good change, whereas back dash cancel is still better, due to it being faster and easier to create space. BUT, none of that matters, because you can't get away from anything, as I said moves reach so far and your back dashes are tiny, slow and feel sluggish compared to older games.    But, this is a 3D game so you should side step! Right!? Nope because they've also made side steps useless. Actually, wait they IMPROVED side step in S2! Except, they also improves everyone's tracking on moves and added new homing moves. So, basically it's even worse now. A 3D game that plays like a 2D game.  There is nothing unique about any character anymore, but also remember how there were some, handful, characters that weren't really good (and some good) but they had that one thing, that made them stand out from the rest? Like a weapon and some spiritual/magic stuff or characters that had cool stance options and or guard break moves; Well guess what it's all still there! Except now EVERYONE has them! All the characters are so homogenised, the same applies for the players, every player/person plays the same.  Heat system is actually nice feature, essentially a hype button activated, but implemented poorly. First of all, it does this goofy zoom in every. Time. Someone. Activates. Heat. Whenever I took a break from Tekken 7, I felt refreshed and re-engergize to improve my skill set, but Tekken 8 doesn't give me any sort of accomplishment and satisfaction. Everything felt artificial, almost all my  wins are due to the game's oppressive style over a strong defense that many players have honed for years.   In Tekken 7, being aggressive may result in opponent outmaneuvering you, and tiny little things like Korean Back Dash, sidestep and various Tekken fundamentals are what determines what kind of player you are. Tekken 8 removed many of those fundamentals and normalize all the characters. Everyone has a running + moves, everyone has a stance mixups, everyone have the same gameplan, everything just felt the same.  Despite Tekken 7's final 3 seasons catering to an offensive gameplan, it never felt as overwhelmed as Tekken 8, and special effects are one of the biggest gripe I have with this game, I just can't cant see ♥♥♥♥. Whenever I go back and watch some Tekken 7 footage, its just visually cleaner and much easier to digest.   I'm not here to say Tekken 8 is game that has no redeeming qualities, but when your core design of the game has changed, your audience will be shifting as well. I truly hope season 3 will fix the various issues that we avid Tekken players have asked for. But I find it hard to believe it as the team decided not to do anything about it after some few fixes. I am not someone who usually write reviews for a game, but Tekken has always been a game I've play daily on both PC and Playstation. It's my first time playing a Tekken, and I have to admit that I find it fun that each character has their own fighting style and combos. Some combat dynamics are great, but there is something that bothers me a lot, and that is that Bandai Namco doesn't make an effort to retain new players. First of all, several characters (if not many) are ridiculously unbalanced. By just spamming a couple of buttons with those characters, you can even achieve a perfect. Some moves and hitboxes are absurdly weird (I'm talking about you, Alisa and Yoshimitsu), and there are characters that are too complicated to even counter or parry, like King. Many times, you can't even put into practice what you learned in tutorials because the opponent doesn't even let you stand up after spamming the same two attacks. If only they balanced the characters and made some technical adjustments, I feel the game would be more enjoyable for new players.  Another thing that I found annoying was the enormous number of smurfs in quick match and ranked games. They pair you a lot with accounts that have no ratings and the default 100 points, but when you fight them, those players seem like they came straight from EVO. I understand that sometimes you lose or have a losing streak, but it's not even close to normal to see people with default accounts having 7 or even 9 consecutive wins without it being reflected in their accounts. I think I could understand it if it were about playing ranked matches because we've all been ambitious and want to win, but it's too boring to fight people who clearly already have experience with the game that just want hunting rookies in categories that are technically for beginners and new players.  I don’t understand how Namco expects to attract new audiences and players to Tekken if they technically do nothing to prevent veteran players from scaring off rookies for feeling superior with their techniques and combos. They should improve their matching system. Anyway, I recommend the game for playing with friends; the online can sometimes be stressful or tedious if you want play alone.

Tekken players all agree certain aspects of the games design are fundamentally flawed, and overlook them hoping the game will change for the better. Tekken devs double down on their mistakes and make the game fundamentally worse, alienating players more. Despite the failure of Soul Calibur 6, Bandai Namco and it's tragically misled team have decided to carry it's worst problems into tekken. Instead of focusing on the rich complexities of the game, we are being drowned in system mechanics that are designed to make it easier for people who simply do not care about it.  The roster is full of duds who wouldn't see play if it wasn't for them being overtuned to have "competitive" value. Most of the cast has been flanderized into "emotionless stick of wood" or "guffawing joke idiot". The story is nonsense, and mostly still boring. The actual archetypes of characters have been eroded to ensure most players can swap without adapting their play style much, because ultimately there is only one playstyle; aggressive. This is the keyword of tekken 8's design philosophy as expressed by it's devs many times. The focus on creating an aggressive game has led them to make a game where defense is heavily punished. Chip damage on guard, chip damage on throw breaks, insane plus frame attacks on guard, all designed to stop players from feeling rewarded for maintaining a solid defense, and instead encourage them to take needless risks and gamble arbitrarily.  Multiplayer content aside, the games weird AI training "ghost" battle BS is absurd, and the single player content is mostly boring.   When you take the colossal failures of tekken 8 in all at once, it paints a picture of a company desperately trying to appeal to the lowest common denominator, in any way possible. EDIT:  Everything has, dare I say it, been going smoothly for the last few patches. The game is going in a better direction and it's the best it's been since release imo. If they keep it up I'll keep it positive. I'm leaving my old complaints however to remind people what we had to deal with and if we're not careful, what we'll have to deal with again.  I am definitely in the camp of enjoying this game a lot and even love it sometimes, but it has a lot of decisions that make me question the competence and sanity of the designers. I'm really into the game competitively and dive into it quite a bit deeper than the average player so I tend to get familiar with the game's inner workings; so when I see so many exceptions to rules to an absurd degree it makes my head hurt.  Again I totally agree that the game needs to be criticized harshly especially with the horrifying U-Turn they took in S2 directly towards a more toxic, volatile game, and the absolute radio silence for 6 plus months is ridiculous. Unfortunately I'm stuck still enjoying the game even with all of it's stupid flaws and stupid decisions, because there just is NOT a game like this anywhere. VF is too old and outdated for me and I will 100% play the new one when it comes out but for 3D fighters there's just no competition to be found.  Many people mention "ugh constant 50/50 at all times" but I think it goes much deeper than that. 50/50 is an important fundamental part of all fighting games; there HAS to be a mixup at some point to open up the opponent, otherwise holding back at all times is just an option select to any offence. Now I think people need to specify and focus their dislike of 50/50's, namely the easy access to them with relatively low risk.  If I'm going to put you into a situation where you have to guess the mixup or eat a bunch of damage, I should have to work for it. I should need to condition you to block first so even a slow move will make you hesitate, or make you whiff, or punish you first with something other than a 10f. I should not be able to just mindlessly run across the screen with a big, homing while running mid and make you guess for your life because you didn't react to the 20 frame move (a third of a second, quick reminder how fast that is) with a jab or sidestep. I also should not be able to put you into a guess or die situation off a 10f punish, that idea is stupid as hell because that means you cannot take ANY risks against me or you're not only going to eat the guaranteed punish, but you're going to be mixed up for daring to use the least unsafe option possible while not being outright safe. Personally, I believe 12f punishes should be the minimum for a hard mixup situation, especially from stance.  To top it all off because I can keep going on about this for so long I'll write a thesis; I know they wanted to up the aggression and make it less backdash and whiff focused like T7 which is understandable, but gutting backdash to this extent is too much. I shouldn't be able to backdash out of any mixup situation granted, but if I block a move that's, say, -4 on block, and the opponent mashes something afterwards, I should be able to quickly backdash out of the way to avoid immediate retaliation. The opponent then has to use half a brain cell to use a longer range linear move or dash forward before continuing their pressure, creating mind games and counterplay. As it stands, backdashing is rarely an option even on block, and only on some characters do you have strong backdashes, others barely move. A small buff to backdash along with a slight reduction to constant forward movement when attacking, I believe, would help lessen volatility.  Their buffs to sidesteps have been steps in the right direction for sure, but it's counteracted by their addition of ridiculous new moves in S2 that cover character weaknesses for no reason, and the infamous wonky hitboxes and re-aligning strings that even when you whiff let you just press an attack and turn back around to continue hitting your opponent. I'm thinking of a couple of specific characters when I say this but I don't want to make this a character balance issue, more of a systemic issue.  TL;DR I love the game but it has a lot of highly questionable decisions that make it far too volatile and difficult to deal with. I understand their desire to make comebacks and even lesser skilled players able to compete, but as of right now it's taken to an absurd degree that severely frustrates players that do not have the "I MUST MASH CONSTANTLY" mindset. Defensive play, while plausible and can be done, is VERY difficult to execute in order to compete with even an intermediate player, as it takes ten times the knowledge, reflexes and execution to be defensive than offensive. I also have not touched on the lackluster story mode, single player arcade content, or lackluster customization. Hell, even their PAID stuff is often mid or just not worth the money and just screams laziness and greed.  As it stands right now, I cannot recommend this game because so far the developers have not shown that they are in touch with the general sentiment of the playerbase and want to cater to the super casuals, which with respect, are not the bread and butter that keeps the franchise alive. If they take steps to make the game less volatile and casino-like I will change my review to a positive one, until then, I cannot in good faith reward their bad behavior.

this one sits oddly and has a weird barrier for entry skill requirement than the previous games. in some aspects, the game is easier and more lenient on execution heavy inputs which allows for people with not a lot of time and dedication on their hands to play the game at a decent level, but at the same time eliminating the flaws characters had in previous installments.. this makes Tekken 8 a game where knowledge checks and +frame mixup pressure easily win you games if you aren't a pro or have fundamental skills from other Tekken games.   on the surface, this isn't a bad thing, but in the first season and even well into season 2, defense is still taking a backseat compared to everyone's offense. at higher levels of skill, however, you cannot get away with a lot of cheese and you need to revert back to fundamentals from previous games to SOME level.. it's just not as necessary as it was in Tekken 7 and before. i've been playing Tekken since 2009 irc with Tekken 6 on the Xbox, i dont consider myself a pro, but i do have legacy knowledge. with the addition of more complex characters and movesets comes more homework for you and your opponent, needing to remember every string or frame trap to be able to reliably deal with early rank cheese. you're not compelled to play carefully against people most of the time, as they will do their usual flowcharts and expect you to mash. since the damage is so high, you wont be able to adapt mid-match as much as you could from previous games.   if you are planning to play Tekken 8, please dont be discouraged from playing after seeing the move lists. allow your brain and body to build muscle-memory, practice using your tools and punishes correctly.. and most importantly, do not sweat misinputing. most people cannot even do King's chain throws, let alone electrics.   tl;dr: lower barrier to entry but overall higher skill ceiling; average experience is flowcharting and doing 50/50 mixups to win. take your time and adjust accordingly if you want to try it out.

Review for Tekken 8 (Ultimate Edition) – Buyer Beware  I’m a long-time fan of the Tekken series and was excited to support the latest installment by purchasing the Tekken 8 Ultimate Edition. However, I’m extremely disappointed with what “Ultimate” actually means here.  When you label something as an Ultimate Edition, it implies that you're getting the complete experience — all future DLC, characters, stages, costumes, etc. That’s standard across the industry, and many of us bought this edition in good faith, expecting full content coverage.  Instead, Bandai Namco has now released a Season 2 which is not included in the Ultimate Edition. So what exactly did we pay a premium for? Turns out it only covers Season 1 — a fact that wasn't clearly communicated during the game's launch or in the edition's description at the time.  This is misleading marketing. If you're only getting Season 1 content, it should have been labeled something like “Complete Season 1 Edition” — not “Ultimate.” Naming it otherwise feels intentionally deceptive and designed to squeeze more money out of loyal fans down the line.  I don’t blame Steam for this. The blame lies squarely with Bandai Namco for pushing a false sense of value. As it stands, the Ultimate Edition is not worth the price if future seasons are going to be sold separately.  Very disappointed.

So, I bought this game because I am a fan of tekken franchise. I played Tekken 2, Tekken 3, Tekken 5, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, Tekken 7, and now this Tekken 8.  I was already disappointed with Tekken 7. But I have to say that Tekken 8 is complete garbage, an absolute waste of money. The game is heavily unbalanced, cheats and exploits are common, and what made tekken different from other fighting games has been completely removed in this one. Tekken 8 is a fighting game as many others, and arguably the worst tekken game in the franchise and the worst fighting game out there,  Tekken 8 uses a heat system and rage art system. The rage art system is completely unbalanced and terrible. I understand the idea behind it, but it is horrible. This is also why Tekken 7 honestly sucked. But the heat system is the worst: it advantages characters that are inherently aggressive, such as Brian. However, characters that are slow or with slow animations, or that are inherently defensive or that use primarily counters are incredibly disadvantaged.   The game is absolute trash for this price. I regret buying it. The only positive thing is that it is flashy and what not. Besides this, it is a terrible game.  A tip for Jun players: Jun, in this game, is definitely better compared to how she was in Tekken Tag Tournament 2. However, Jun results to be bad nonetheless. Why? Simple. The design of the character seemed to be that she had the capability of regenerating her health bar with certain moves, and that could benefit of the heat system by recharging her health, besides of course using amazing counters. There's a problem: every character restores health, with or without heat system, at the same rate Jun does, in practice. One could argue "but Jun can restore health beyond the white bar", yeah, but the amount that she restores is negligible. Second problem, Jun's damage is low compared to the damage that certain characters, such as Devil Jin or Heihachi, can deal on a single hit. Third problem, like in Tekken 7, there is "armor", i.e. moves that momentarily make the character shine and that cannot be stopped, unless one uses a low hit or a throw. I think the armour system is often abused by a lot of players, making the game practically unplayable with certain characters. Fourth problem, Jun gets staggered by almost every hit from aggressive characters, unlike other characters. So, it is significantly more difficult to punish with Jun compared to punishing with, in practice, any other character. Finally, fifth problem... Jun is slow as hell in this game. She is the slowest character of the game as far as I am concerned. Her move animations are quite long, and they can be interrupted by faster characters with shorter hit animations (namely, any other character, since most characters can produce a strike in 0.1 ms, compared to Jun that often takes between 0.3 and 0.8 ms from button input).    Note on Yoshimitsu: Yoshimitsu's counter can counter everything and stagger, namely it can counter low hits, high hits, and throws. I think it is a bit busted and unbalanced.   Note on Heihachi and similar characters that, to be used, need to be bought separately: I wouldn't say they are "pay to win" characters, because that's not the case. However, they definitely come with some incredible moves that, in my opinion, can be heavily abused by players, and increased damage. For instance, Fakhumram, the new released character, can punish from great distances of the ring... I find it a bit odd and somewhat heavily unbalanced.   Final thought: I truly hope the makers of this game have a huge loss in terms of sales, because this game is just terrible, a waste of money, and not so entertaining at all, but more frustrating than anything else.

High level players will intentionally create new accounts and fail their placement matches for rank so that they will start at the bottom with all the other low level players. Then they farm the low level players for rank on that character, then rinse and repeat. I have played every single Tekken since the very first one, each one thousands of hours, and by far the worst one of them all is Tekken 8. Sure, it looks good, has very good production value etc, but outside of all that - the actual game itself, it is just bad and I am tired of pretending that it is not. Bandai Namco likes to gaslight the player base - it wasn't bad netcode, it was YOUR bad internet. It is not bad game, it is YOUR skill issue etc, while in fact - it is the game. Everything is for the offense. Skill ceiling is destroyed, there is nothing to lab anymore, since everything follows, moves, tracks, is plus and launchers. Everything is a 25 second combo, everything takes you to the wall and all walls sticks like a fly paper. Everything auto corrects, so at this point this game might as well just be fully AI, no need for any player, because essentially you are just watching cut scenes and not really playing. So many long animations that interrupt the flow. Even basic knockdowns have built in followups into guaranteed oki, that cannot be avoided. Risk-reward is like 9 to 1 in favor of the attacker. All defensive tools are removed or nerfed, so you just have to guess. Tekken 8 is a casino, where you just have to be lucky. Never has there been a Tekken game where max rank is filled with player with 0 knowledge about the  game, movement, later movement, ducking etc, because you can just keep mashing since plus, plus, plus, mid, mid, launcher, launcher, no execution. This game is hell on training wheel and a perfect example when 12-year olds design a game thinking "lets give everyone everything with no drawbacks", so it will be fun fun fun. If this game frustrated you - don't worry, the problem is not you, but the game. It punishes skill, time and patience, rewards recklessness and fast brain dead rewards. Utterly disgusting and sad remnant of a franchise that used to be the best fighting game in history.

In S2 they apologized and said the S2 patch failed and did not go in their intended direction. "We will take all your feedback very serious" Nakatsu wrote. Players who were dissatisfied stuck out the whole S2 with the hopes for S3, even if the devs slogan "we can not make changes during tournament season for the competitors sake" sounded cheap, especially when even pro players in the tournaments wanted system changes to make their situation less stressful.  Cue to S3 getting closer. The devs used a Tekken dog whistle and said "S3 will go back to basics"; everyone smokes hopium. Is S3 as bad as S2? No, S2 is the worst in Tekken. Season 3 is sort of "season 2.2" if you will, some needed nerfs to the most unfair S2 characters, some buffs and 2 system changes (one buggy, i.e. heat smash wall splats if you whiff the first hit. S3 is the disappointing patch, the letdown, the realization that we are being lied to and hopefully the exodus of the playerbase so the devs learn. I do not hope for the latter though. Original review: Having come back to this game for the third time as of writing this, I really want to like this game but I don't. The focus on aggressiveness is not fun to me. Heat as a get out of jail card without any risk, rage art as a semi get out of jail card, power crush as a get out of jail card, auto parries as a get out of jail card, stances with auto parries as a get out of jail card, the overuse of stance and install based character overhauls, lack of poking, lack of movement, chip damage from mashing your face on the controller, guard breaking moves, unblockable moves, teleporting moves on characters, guns/weapon moves on characters, projectiles on characters, exploding stage hazards, emphasis on forced 50/50 mixups, the simplification of the cast neglecting the hours spent by players to master aspects of a character (e.g. Law's DDS or Drag's WR2), cast being stripped of their flaws by getting moves that are a mix of mids/lows that are plus on block, homing, heat activating, counter hit launching, power crushing and active from range 3 (or full screen almost). All because the dev team designed a character that had a specific set of flaws but in this game decided that said flaws "made it difficult for *insert your character here* at the particular situation". Overtuned characters and a general homogenization of it.  High level Tekken is less interesting to watch since they are forced to constantly press buttons to not get overwhelmed by the opponent.  The aesthetic is too much. The particle effects makes the game look worse and at times it is hard to see what is going on. No option given to turn it off locally. Yes, Tekken has had influences from fantasy/anime before but Tekken 8 doubles down on this for some reason. Every character shoots laser and lightning out of their ass and spouts annoying nonsense to a larger degree than in Tekken 7, it is baffling. The rage arts are ridiculous flashy short movies. Stages follows this trend and many look oversaturated, making it difficult to see the characters. Getting juggled allows one to take a five minute stretch. New combos are added that makes the game look even dumber and take even longer time (e.g. Jim and pigeon Jim in S2).  There is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ monetization practices and annoying collaborations forced upon the game post launch. The DLC decisions to lock knowledge check monsters needing to be labbed (e.g. Eddy, Lidia) behind DLC or adding mismatched characters (Clive) to the game and acting all surprised when the character focused on martial arts from the same franchise, that have been requested since Tekken 7, was neglected.   I wanted a game with the clean look of previous Tekkens with a focus on the martial arts, movement, reading your opponent and slowly growing as a player from putting in the hours. Tekken 8 does not provide that. I had problems with the game in S1 and S2 just doubled down on the aspects I do not like. No, Tekken 7 was not a perfect game by any means but the parts that I did not like about it, often found in the different DLC characters, seems to have been the base that Tekken 8 was built from. If you have never played a Tekken game before and want to give this game a try, then go ahead and form your own opinion of it. If it is your first experience with the franchise you might enjoy it, especially if you have friends to play with. It is not a bad game, only a disappointing "Tekken" that has gone in the direction I did not want to.  In the end I am the clown for coming back to the game yet again, just because I want to play a 3D fighter and thus try to force enjoyment out of this game. Bandai won't have to bother with adjusting anything no matter how much I and others complain if they are satisfied and we keep coming back to play this game and keeping the player count up. I had some really high hopes coming from Tekken 7, but I just cannot faithfully recommend getting into Tekken 8 due to the developers' direction with the game until the game gets a major overhaul or tuning to its current fight system.  The pivot towards offensive-heavy gameplay through the new Heat system, forced stance transitions, 50/50s, and +on block moves with very few options to respond defensively (given that even the buffs to sidestep/sidewalk in Season 2 don't help much) makes the game more frustrating. Combos are egregiously long as well, despite the increase to health in an attempt band-aid fix this issue.  In addition to the previous, many characters also either unnecessarily gained/lost new moves/properties covering their historical weaknesses, which contributed to the uniqueness for each character but now further blurs the lines of individuality and skill expression.  Overall, the game feels less calculated, frustrating, and lost the feeling of being genuinely skill-checked by more knowledgeable players due to the offensive gameplay pivot compared to Tekken 7. You don't feel like you're genuinely learning anything either since you have to cater your gameplan to the offense and 50/50s.

Some people will probably not like my take on this and fighting games but honestly I don't care. Fighting games are in a bad spot in terms of popularity with exactly one exception right now being Street Fighter 6. Tekken and Street fighter used to be direct competitors and now Tekken just falls to obscurity as well as many other titles. I want fighting games to be better and have more people playing them but as most of them are right now I just don't have much interest.  Pros:  The game looks fantastic. (This cannot be overstated visually incredible)  One of the only 3D competitive fighters so it feels unique  Long standing Characters that people recognize and care about  Actually reworked older characters to attempt to make the game more accessible (will discuss this in further detail)  Neutrals:  Cosmetic System is simultaneously fantastic and stupid at the same time (Just let people disable seeing everyone's cosmetics for several reasons like not seeing outfits that could theoretically offend them/ being distracted)  Crossover Characters (You would think this would be good or bad but its more nuanced its good for the growth of the game but typically you get annoying characters like Mr.John Fantasy)  Cons:  Needlessly Complex and unappealing to the vast majority of newcomers ( I have several friends who have been interested in playing Tekken 8 since launch and opted to either not play a fighting game at all or buy Street Fighter instead. All of them cite the exact same thing when they made their decision as they learned more about Tekken "Its just way to much")  Older Fans Gatekeeping their game and keeping it worse because they complain when things get easier (The community in this game revolves around wanting everyone else to suffer like they had to and complaining saying they have to work harder than everyone since their character is low tier etc)  Lackluster alternate game modes and lacking multiple previous game modes to give variety to the game (Tekken 7 Bowling as an example)  Objectively terrible Monetization structure ( Committing the grievous act of having all 3 forms of monetization because the game isn't keeping as many players so it needs more money per player to stay alive Buying the game at full price subscription in the form of battle passes and micro transactions in the form of cosmetics and DLC Characters which i will detail more about in the next point)  DLC Character Syndrome (Almost every single Fighting game that has Paid DLC characters suffers from this problem to a degree. They are incentivized to make them extremely strong so you are more likely to purchase them which reduces enjoyment for players that just want to play the characters they like.)  In conclusion I am not good at fighting games nor am I a novice. I have hundreds of hours in several fighting games but Tekken is the only one where after 100 hours I still feel like I know absolutely nothing there are way too many little things to learn making the barrier to entry far too high. I personally believe that if Tekken doesn't become more accessible it will continue on its trend into obscurity and maybe fail to capture enough people to justify further titles. I love the way the game looks and a lot of aspects of how it feels. I would hate to see the game go down this route. Please improve your game stop gatekeeping newer players out of being interested Tekken will die whether you like it or not.

This game's biggest problem is not what issues it shares with all modern fighting games: predatory monetization of all aspects, weak defensive options, aggressive and oppressive offense, system mechanics that interrupt the gameflow, issues with its lateral movement due to an overabundance of attacks that track movement, and so on.   The biggest issue that I have only encountered in Tekken 8 is the lack of decision-making from the developers and the behavior of its community. Not forcing people to undergo a benchmark regarding both graphical and network performance means that almost every match suffers from unintentional or intentional stuttering and lag. And if that wasn't enough of a bummer, running into a parade of players not rematching regardless of the outcome for hours on end is just baffling. Neither in SF6, GGST, nor any other fighting game have I seen such a messy netcode and players who don't want to play the game.  What even is the point of playing the game if no one is willing to play the game and/or is actively trying to make it worse for the other people involved?  The only question that remains is if it is worth it to trudge through hours of bad matches just to chase that unbelievable high that happens when everything falls into place. The core identity of Tekken — the skill-based mind games, movement, and legacy mechanics — feels completely abandoned. Heat System: A gimmick that destroys pacing and rewards button mashing over skill. Balance: Characters feel unpolished, with broken tools and unfair matchups. Movement Nerfs: Sidestepping and backdashing, which made Tekken unique, are gutted. Casualization: It feels like this was made for highlight reels and casual players, not the loyal fanbase who carried Tekken for decades. Now no one talks about that.  That's because there is no sick movement.  Everything has been stripped away.  Your backdash doesn't do anything, and 80% of the match you're flooded with unreasonable plus frames.  Even if you wanted to move around you can't.  Why learn how to backdash cancel when you can just mash back, and get Walmart backdash cancel.    What type of character do you want to main? Doesn't really matter they're all the same!  All of the characters have everything a character could ever want for.  This makes them all feel and play the same.  There seems to be some sort of obsession with stances. Well just pick whatever character you want and shoot yourself in the foot by not using their stance.  The animations and movesets are so overdramatic and anime it makes every fight look so corny.  Blinding particle effects, characters flying back and forth across the screen, and swords and guns doing whatever.  Tekken has lost its identity and we've ended up with this sloppy mess of a game. There is nothing at the top of the mountain, you don't get to play awesome and look awesome while doing it. Review Tekken 8 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐   Tekken 8 is without a doubt one of the most exciting and polished entries in the legendary fighting game franchise. Bandai Namco has truly delivered a game that feels modern, fast, and visually stunning, while still staying true to the roots that long-time fans love. From the moment you boot it up, it’s clear this is a celebration of the series’ history and a bold step forward for competitive fighters.  Pros  Spectacular Visuals: The graphics are some of the best in any fighting game to date. Character models, stages, and effects look incredibly detailed, bringing every punch, kick, and special move to life.  Fluid Combat: The fighting feels smoother and more dynamic than ever. The new Heat System adds an exciting layer of strategy that rewards aggression and creativity.  Character Variety: The roster is well-balanced and diverse, offering both fan favorites and fresh faces. Each character feels unique with their own style and personality.  Story Mode: The cinematic presentation makes the story engaging and impactful, adding emotional weight to the long-standing Mishima saga.  Online Play with Cross-Play: A huge win! Tekken 8 finally brings cross-play, making it easier than ever to fight friends and rivals no matter what platform they’re on.  Accessibility: With simplified control options, newcomers can jump in without feeling overwhelmed, while veterans still have all the depth and complexity they crave.  Cons (Room for Improvement)  Balancing Tweaks Needed: Some characters and moves may feel slightly overpowered in the early days, but this can be fine-tuned with patches.  More Single-Player Content: While the story is strong, additional modes, challenges, or arcade-style extras would give solo players more reasons to keep coming back.  Customization Variety: Character customization is good but could use even more depth and creativity to truly stand out.  Learning Curve: Although accessible, mastering Tekken 8 still requires dedication. A more robust tutorial system could help beginners ease into advanced techniques.  And yes… I miss Lucky Chloe: Tekken 7’s dancing queen was goofy, flashy, and fun — I’m crossing my fingers she moonwalks back into Tekken 8 someday!  Final Thoughts  Tekken 8 is a powerhouse of a fighting game that pushes the series into a new era. It’s beautiful, fast, and fun — perfect for both casual players and competitive fans. While there’s always room to grow with future updates and DLC, what’s here at launch is already fantastic. This game feels like a love letter to fighting game fans and a clear sign that Tekken remains one of the kings of the genre.  Reviewed by Zulandin from Zul TV on YouTube and TikTok

Tekken 8 Review: The King Is Back, and He's a Beast  Listen up, fighting game fans. Tekken 8 isn't just a new game; it's a statement. Tekken 7 brought the series back to life, but Tekken 8 is here to push the genre into a whole new era. With jaw-dropping visuals, a super aggressive new combat system, and a story that feels like a full-on movie, this game blew my expectations out of the water.  Looks and Vibe Right from the jump, the first thing you notice is how damn good Tekken 8 looks. Built on Unreal Engine 5, every character model, stage, and special effect is packed with insane detail. You can see the sweat on Jin's face, the fiery glow from Kazuya's moves, and even individual snowflakes falling in the Siberia stage. The stages are dynamic and destructible, which just amps up the drama and makes every fight feel like a cinematic showdown. The music is also fire—a mix of rock, electronic, and orchestral tracks that get your blood pumping the second the match starts.  The New Combat System Tekken has always been about deep 3D combat, and Tekken 8 takes that to the next level with the Heat system. This is the core of the game and what makes it feel so fresh. By activating a Heat Burst or Heat Engager, your character enters a 'Heat' state for a few seconds. In this state, you can use a Heat Dash to extend combos or a Heat Smash for a powerful finisher.  The Heat system pushes you to be more aggressive. It's not just about waiting for an opening; it's about going on the offensive and creating your own chances. Combos that used to be a nightmare are now easier to pull off, which makes the game more welcoming for newcomers. For the veterans, it adds a whole new layer of strategy. Managing your Heat becomes a huge part of dominating a fight.  They also brought in the Tornado mechanic, which replaces the old Bound system from Tekken 7. Tornado lets you launch opponents high into the air, setting them up for some sick combos. This, along with the return of Rage Arts, makes the pace of the game feel fast and frantic. Every hit feels impactful, and every combo is super satisfying.  Story Mode: A Blockbuster Experience One of the most impressive things about Tekken 8 is its story mode, "The Dark Awakens." After years of fighting, the clash between Jin Kazama and Kazuya Mishima finally comes to a head. The story is full of drama, plot twists, and epic cinematic fights that feel like something straight out of a Hollywood movie. The cutscenes are gorgeous, and the voice acting is on point, pulling you deep into the emotional narrative.  The story mode is a great way to get a feel for the game's mechanics in a real-world setting. While the story might be a bit cheesy for some, the execution is so good that it stands as one of the best story modes in any fighting game.  Besides the main story, there are also Character Episodes that give you a deeper look into each fighter's backstory. It's a great way to get to know your favorite characters and see how they fit into the bigger Tekken world.  Content and Replay Value Tekken 8 is stacked with content. Besides the story mode, you've got Arcade Quest, which helps new players learn the ropes, and the Tekken Fight Lounge, a 3D social hub where you can hang out with other players, have casual matches, or just watch fights.  The training and tutorial modes are top-tier. The Tekken 8 Practice Mode is one of the best I've ever seen, with easy-to-read frame data, combat simulations, and customizable training scenarios. It's an invaluable tool for anyone looking to get better.  And for all you fashionistas out there, the character customization is insane. You can find all kinds of cosmetic items—from costumes to accessories—to make your favorite fighter totally unique.  Final Thoughts Tekken 8 is the peak of 3D fighting games. It nails the perfect balance between keeping the old school feel and adding awesome new stuff. The mind-blowing visuals, aggressive combat, and cinematic story make this a must-buy.  Whether you've been playing Tekken since the PlayStation 1 days or you're new to the genre, Tekken 8 has something for everyone. This is a game you'll love playing, learning, and mastering. Every fight is a blast, and you'll feel the energy and adrenaline that makes Tekken 8 so special.  If you're looking for a game that's deep, engaging, and visually stunning, Tekken 8 is it. It's a masterpiece that not only respects its past but also confidently steps into the future.  Overall Score: Highly Recommended

Opinion of a 35 year old Azucena main (Tekken King on Xbox and PC.) Also this is my first Tekken game since Tekken 3, and honestly I was a child at that time lol. I've played a lot of fighting games over the years, and  gotten pretty good on a casual level, but this is the first game I've truly tried to learn and be good at. So, some may say i'm a scrub, and some may say i'm still a noob. Anyways, this is not only my favorite Tekken, but it's also my favorite fighting game. I've spent thousands of hours on Xbox learning, and grinding. I've met countless friends, and spent hours scrubbing it out and conversing as we learn the match-ups and deep mechanics of this game. It's a very hard game to learn, and there will be growing pains. You will get perfects done to you. You will struggle with character match-ups. You have to learn and study to find your way in dealing with large move lists, and a variety of different play styles. It's all been worth it. If you stick with it you will eventually stop fighting against characters, and you will finally start fighting the pilot. Then the flow of Tekken will start becoming what I consider a work of art. It's a fighting game with so many mechanics and moves, and in the hands of good players it's just some of the most satisfying gameplay a fighting game can offer. If you are the pilot it gives you such a satisfying rush to break down someones fighting style, and then dismantle their defense into a 100+ damage combo. The FGC is divided it seems on this game for various reasons. Personally, I think the devs have made an amazing game. It will never be perfect for everyone, but I trust that the devs are doing their best to make Tekken 8 the best it can be. Things will be broken sometimes, some things may be unbalanced sometimes, and characters can be over tuned. Underneath it all is a fighting game that I consider the best in it's class, and I will be here to ride the wave until the end. I've made some great memories through this game. If you're reading this, I hope you chose to do the same also. Win or lose, trash talk or respect. I look forward to seeing everyone in the que.

Why Tekken 8 Fails the Legacy of Fighting Games (Review from a Bushin Jin)  Main Character: Jin Kazama Highest Rank Achieved: Bushin (Top ~5% of global players) Time Played: 100+ Hours  I am a 51-year-old gamer who grew up on the arcade and early console era of fighting games, where fundamentals actually meant something. I am not writing this review out of rage or after a bad loss streak; I am writing it after successfully grinding to the elite blue ranks, analyzing the system, and deciding to permanently uninstall the game for my own mental health.  If you are a working adult with a family and limited free time, or if you love traditional fighting games that reward spatial awareness, patient defense, and human-to-human reads, stay far away from Tekken 8.  Here is a breakdown of why this game is fundamentally flawed:  1. The System-Enforced "Unga Bunga" Meta The developers explicitly stated they designed Tekken 8 for "forced aggression." They succeeded, but they completely destroyed tactical depth in the process. Because of the Heat system, massive chip damage on block, and tracking moves that skip the spacing game entirely, pure defense is dead. High-level Tekken 8 is not chess; it is a series of chaotic, forced 50/50 coin flips. Guessing wrong twice shouldn't cost you a round, but in this game's hyper-optimized landscape, it does.  2. A Fraudulent Visual Loop The visual presentation frequently lies to the player. You can physically connect a punch or kick directly into an opponent's face, but because the internal system loop has granted them "priority" mid-combo, your hit becomes invisible, their animation overrides yours, and you are punished for making a correct physical read. A fighting game should accurately reflect its mechanics visually. Tekken 8 forces you to play a frame-data spreadsheet rather than reacting to what your eyes actually see.  3. The Game as a Second Job Older games (and entries like Dead or Alive) allowed you to win on intuition, timing, and fundamentals. Tekken 8 reduces organic fighting to an academic memory test. You are required to lab and memorize frame advantages, combo paths, and tedious matchup strings for a massive roster. If you cannot treat this game like a part-time job, the mechanics actively lock you out of having fun, completely disregarding your actual combat IQ.  Verdict: I reached the top single-digit percentage of the player base, looked at the "forced-aggression" meta, and realized it wasn't a rewarding challenge, it was just an artificial, exhausting cortisol spike. The community's toxic response to honest critique is just the cherry on top of a deeply hostile environment.  I chose my sanity and my family over a digital badge. If you value your peace of mind, do not waste your time or money here. I never thought I would find a game where I have little to nothing good to say about it. Even games I hate, I can find highlights. However, this game lacks anything good. All this game has to offer is 50/50, safe from punish spam into juggles because the DEVs seem to think this is what people like me (a causal) want.   No, we want games that are easy to understand without a controller layout that makes our fingers cry in pain. We want games that we grow with and learn as we play. You learn nothing in this game outside of how to cheese better. What is the point in a fighting game where most players are trying to air launch you with safe moves 90% of the time because that is what the game wants? Where is the fun in a game that rewards mashing safe moves with little to no downside?   Where is the fun in a game that doesn't reward you for spacing because it so happens that they can just throw out another 50/50 safe move whenever you think there is an opening, that this move will send you into a second 50/50 or an air launch, where you will then watch yourself be juggled across the screen because you dared go for a jab verse a 50/50 monkey masher (and I call them that because even a button masher is above the nonsense in this game, and no, I didn't come up with the name).  This game now joins the meaningless list of rare games that I do not recommend. If I was to rate it, this game is a 3/10 at best (closer to a 2/10). Its story is weak, its gameplay is unbalanced and the DEVs seem to not care, and the movesets are so cluttered with things you will never use that it makes it harder to hit the input you want to due to how the controls work, and the fact some horrid inputs are put next to the good ones.  If this game is like £15, and you really, really want to play it... I guess it may be worth your time. But I can tell you the one reason this game sits at a 55% on Steam is because people who have dropped it don't tend to change their scores. If they came back and played again, the score would be much, much lower.  The worst part is that the people the DEVs may hear out (the "Pros") are too busy fighting about who needs nerfs when the entire game needs a rework, and if that doesn't happen, no matter how many nerfs you get, the core problems of the game will continue to create new broken things that need nerfing  So, as I said, I do not recommend this to anyone; be this people who love fighting games or casuals like me.
