Currently things are looking a lot better. The last few patches have been great and new characters have been quite well balanced as well. Devs are fixing a lot of the major issues the community has had with the game since launch, many of which I mentioned in the previous review (still below). Things are looking bright for the future of the game. I'm actually enjoying the game a lot now.  ---  Old review (Before Season 3):  TL;DR  Sadly Tekken 8 is not fun anymore for a player like me. Trying to improve is a nightmare due to massive system and game design changes that appear to be catering to absolute beginners at the cost of pro play and especially so for the average player looking to get good.  If you want to just play the story and dabble a bit with combos and online, the game is great and everything around that has never been better. If that's what Tekken means to you, you'll love Tekken 8. But I'm writing this from the point of view of me. I'm an average skilled ranked player who tries to improve and learn. I was around purple ranks in Tekken 7 and it was hard getting there. My playstyle is more defensive and movement focused. I spent a lot of time practicing movement and other "fundamentals".  Game looks and sounds great. There's new additions to game modes and practice functionality that is top notch, but there's very little replay value anywhere outside online. Online is fun with friends and casual play, but a nightmare for taking seriously, due to how oppressive offense is now. Backdashing has been all but removed. Without match-up knowledge it's just about who can attack first and better. Defense is now only effective for the absolute top tier players who want to spend absurd hours practicing match-ups, and even then there's a lot of pure guessing where there used to be option selecting and using movement to defend.   ---  This is really sad to write as I love the franchise.  Tekken 8 is brutal and not in a good way like it used to be. Unless you know each match-up pretty well, you're just gonna get killed by offensive stances, which pretty much every character now has, or by plus on block moves into more, or by otherwise blatantly overtuned moves, or by free combos through the new heat system, character specific power-ups, or guard breaks who pretty much everyone seems to have now etc. Pretty much all characters have been dumbed down and execution requirements removed to the point where a toddler can run pretty decent offense on most of the cast. The downside is that countering that offense requires more of you than ever before, making offense incredibly potent. Most matches from absolute beginner to the upper ranks are decided by who can just do better button mashing, which to me is a complete antithesis to what Tekken is all about. If you enjoy party games where you can just press buttons and lots of effects happen on the screen, Tekken is pretty close to that now.  There's no backdashing anymore. Pretty much all moves and strings advance so much that backdashing only makes it possible to get hit by their mids with little to no upside. A lot of strings have mix-ups built in. So good luck learning any counter-play as the opponent can just choose another version of the same string that shuts down any possibility for counter-play. One upside to movement is that sidestepping has been improved in Season 2, which feels great. The problem is that they also added so many good homing moves - of which a lot are launchers - that sidestepping is often a death sentence.  And god forbid if you get launched. Combos last 20 seconds now and every character gets wall-to-wall carry into wall combo and disgusting oki. So most rounds are decided by a launch into guessing for your life. None of that option selecting stuff, just pure guess.  So all in all, the game has devolved into mashing and 50/50's on an unprecedented scale. This sadly is reflected even at the highest level of play where neutral is not seen for the most of the time. It's just 20 seconds of pressure from one side into a guess from the defender and if they guess right, it's 20 seconds of pressure and guessing games for the other.  If all you do is play with a good group of people you know, private lobbies are still fun. But if your main goal is playing ranked and trying to improve, I can't recommend the game with a good conscience. Ranked is just not fun anymore.  And the eSports scene is pretty boring too. Heck, the biggest tournament of the year just finished where the top 8 was two of the same disgustingly overpowered character against another where both are just pressing god moves that require no execution to pull off. It was a snooze fest.  The development team are dragging their feet which to me only indicates that this is the direction they want the game to go. There's a lot of echoes of other competitive games where they started making it easier to get wins, in order to lure in the casual players. In the end they always end up making the game absolutely unplayable for anyone wanting to take the game seriously, which sadly puts off many casuals from engaging with the game long term. I really hope this is not the direction they are intending, but that's exactly what it looks like at the moment, and that's extremely disheartening.  The game looks gorgeous. I like that they're adding in new costumes and stuff to buy (Tekken Store) and earn (through a Battle Pass system). The practice functionality is better than it's ever been and they keep building on it which is a huge plus. The story was pretty dope, perhaps the best in the series. There's a new "Arcade Quest" story as well, which kinda teaches you the basics of Tekken which I really enjoyed even as a seasoned player. There's a new "Ghost Battle" system where you can play AI powered CPU opponents that learn from actual players, which is really interesting. You can even play your own Ghosts that learn new stuff from you on the fly. But outside of the stories, Tekken Ball, classic Arcade mode and the AI Ghost battles, but sadly there's very few ways to play the game with replay value. There's no treasure battle, no survival, tekken force etc. Outside of online, the game kinda runs out of offline content after you finish everything once.

I have very mixed feelings about this game.  I started with Tekken 7 (despite its issues: Marduk), and I really enjoyed the defensive play, movement, and spacing. Tekken 8 moves heavily toward aggressive mechanics (Heat system, chip damage) too hard, making it feel less like... what I expect and loved from Tekken. It takes much longer in T8 to experience the strategic, defensive play that I think defines the series compared to T7.  And okay.. let’s talk about the learning curve. I keep hearing people say Tekken 8 is “easier” than Tekken 7. First of all: WHAT? Because I see nothing. If anything, I get knowledge checked way more here, and for the dumbest reasons. Sometimes I feel like I'm being punished for trying to play like a level-headed person instead of a full-blown unga gorilla. Granted, I like games like Guilty Gear Strive (Game Pass Free Trial) and I enjoy some monkey gameplay from time to time. But I don’t come to Tekken for that. This game constantly throws transitions into stances into more stances into more stances. After the 20th stance I’ve seen in a match, I feel like I’ve had enough.  Ooookay, to be fair, the tutorials in Tekken 8 are better cuz mostly because they actually exist, unlike Tekken 7. It’s a step forward, and worth mentioning, especially since proper detailed tutorials are a new invention for fighting games in general. So, cool, here's the medal. It helps, but it doesn’t fix how unnecessarily overwhelming the rest of the game is.  The game itself looks great, has solid netcode, and a decent roster. Still, visually, there's an odd imbalance: male characters have excellent animation quality and detail (though weirdly dry-skinned), while female characters look pretty but overly doll-like and lack expressiveness. SF6 handled this balance way better, making all characters feel expressive and dynamic.  DLC-wise, Season Pass 1 felt forgettable, and Season Pass 2 was even more disappointing... mostly predictable picks that didn't excite me. After seeing what is up on offer... my expectations of Season Pass 3 are VERY low. And if this game ever adds Marduk as DLC? Yeah, that’ll seal the deal for me.  Also, just a personal nitpick: Tekken's male characters aren’t very attractive, and its female characters aren't particularly cool. Other games, like Guilty Gear or Granblue Fantasy Rising, nail character attractiveness way better, even considering they're anime games (though Tekken is pretty anime at this point anyway).  Overall, Tekken 8 feels like polished mechanics stacked awkwardly on legacy systems. It's not a bad game, but for me personally, it just didn't click like how it did with T7 for me.

Tekken 8 – 600 Hours In: A First-Time Player’s Perspective  As someone who came into Tekken 8 fresh — no prior Tekken experience, just raw curiosity and the willingness to grind — I’ve dropped over 600 hours into this game. I wanted to love it. And for a while, I did.  Season 1 felt rough, no doubt. The mechanics were flashy, Heat System felt like a gamble, and damage was through the roof. But at least there was some learning curve, some level of commitment required to climb the ladder. Even when the balancing was questionable, wins still felt like they were earned.  Season 2, though? Somehow worse. The balancing is completely off the rails. The game is now so “beginner-friendly” that it actively rewards button mashing. I get that fighting games need to attract new players, but we’ve gone from helping newcomers to handing them the keys to the kingdom. You can mash your way up the ranks now. It happens. I’ve seen it. I’ve played against it. And worst of all? It works.  Characters like Hwoarang and Anna are absolutely cracked, able to overwhelm with relentless pressure and flowcharts that are way too safe. There’s no risk vs reward when you're rewarded for just pressing buttons faster than your opponent can think. Bryan’s damage output is ridiculous, and it’s getting to the point where one clean read turns into a 70% health swing. That’s not rewarding skill — that’s just bloated numbers on top of unbalanced mechanics.  I’m not complaining because I’m bad. I’ve stuck with this game longer than any other fighter. I’ve practiced, labbed, watched high-level play, and fought through the grind. I’ve earned my frustration. And it’s frustrating to see the game I dedicated myself to turn into something where neutral, spacing, and decision-making are losing value in favor of autopilot offense and spam-heavy strategies.  Accessibility shouldn't mean brainless. You should still need to learn how to play neutral, how to whiff punish, how to condition, how to block under pressure. But in its current state, Tekken 8 feels like it’s punishing players for thinking, and rewarding those who just go full throttle and pray.  There’s still potential. The core of Tekken is amazing — legacy mechanics, mind games, matchup knowledge. But the current direction? It’s not sustainable for serious players. If this is what Tekken 9 will look like too, I might be out.  (I'd still recommend this game to people attempting to get into fighting games, but be ready for that unimaginable Tekken rage to come out)

If your primary way of playing this game is online, I can't recommend the game.  The experience in this game is so fundamentally different offline compared to online its like playing a completely different game.  The netcode is a joke, the connection strength filter does absolutely nothing, online the game forces you to just sit there and watch as you eat mix up after mix up after mix up.  Poor balancing has plagued the game in season two, and the devs have consistently shown no interest in making meaningful changes with only minor changes being made at sporadic intervals. (Most of the season two patches have been poor at best, game breaking at worst.)   The poor balance is exacerbated by the netcode and connectivity issues, making certain characters unbearable to fight online that are otherwise manageable offline.  Unreal Engine 5 bloat and bad optimization also rears its head, which is a shame because the game often works well on lower spec PCs but UE5 gets in the way of that for seemingly no reason.  The game is better offline, but if you wanted to play offline, I think you would be better off with either of the console versions.

It often feels like the developers just have no understanding of what made Tekken a great fighting game. Updates seem random, and the lack of communication and care for the community’s feedback proves how little they seem to care about their player base. Instead of refining mechanics, they’ve managed to strip away what little fun was left for dedicated players.  In all honesty, Tekken 8 is a testament to how not to develop a fighting game. Tekken 8 is the latest instalment in BANDAI NAMCO's long-running Tekken series of arcade-style, 1-on-1 fighting games. This game offers a broad range of unique characters, both newcomers and veterans alike, each with their own fighting style.  This game's newest in-game mechanic is the Heat Meter which, when activated in each round, grants players a temporary boost of power, namely chip damage, and the ability to perform a powerful Heat Burst move. This mechanic can be easily compared to the MAX MODE mechanic in SNK's King of Fighters series.  Tekken 8 also offers a broad range of varied game modes, including the fan-favourite Tekken Ball mode and two new virtual lobby modes: the offline Arcade Quest, and the online Battle Lounge.  Alas, although Tekken 8 has so much content for players old and new alike, the PC version of this game is shockingly bugged and thus almost unplayable, even for players with computers made for gaming.  In particular, Tekken 8 has the longest loading times between matches in Tekken history thus far. In my experience, offline matches often take at least 2 or 3 minutes to load. In all the previous Tekken games, in-game matches only took up 15 seconds to load.  Worse yet, online matchmaking, in my experience, is almost impossible without cross-play. When I first tried out the online Battle Lounge mode, I was only able to play 1 out of 15 online matches, because the other 14 online matches ended up disconnecting for some unknown reason, even when my opponents and I agree to face off with each other.  As a result, it becomes painstakingly clear why many fellow Tekken players feel disappointed with Tekken 8. To add insult to injury, the previous instalment, Tekken 7, ran much more smoothly with faster loading times and accessible online matchmaking.  All in all, Tekken 8 has plenty of content for fighting game fans old and new, but I would not recommend the PC version, not unless you cannot play this game on console and thus you can only play on PC.

I've been following, studying and competing in Tekken for over 10 years at this point. I've always pushed through the difficulties of learning such a complex series and I can appreciate Tekken from both a casual and a competitive perspective. I'm all for having a different change of pace and being able to do different things. However, this is not how you do it properly.  There are good things about this game. I've always liked the visuals, designs and animations and this game is no different. Practice mode has just about anything you need. Matchmaking works well overall. The jukebox feature to change stage music is welcome and I hope it returns for future games.  With that said, everything else is a colossal disappointment. The main issue with the gameplay itself is not one big erroneous mechanic or feature. It's the amalgamation of everything that adds up to a cocktail of absolute chaos and uncertainty, where the game is stressful and uncontrollable for both player and opponent.  If you want to make a game where you have to overwhelm your opponent with offense, that's the developers' vision and I respect that, but if you spoonfeed solutions by adding unreasonably strong moves and systems instead of having the player think to get around a situation or work around a character's weakness, you lose character type variety, play style variety and player intelligence.  The story had potential but it was nonsensical, adding the micro-transaction shop after the game reviews were out was filthy, the balance team is clueless and doesn't know who to listen to or what to do, the combos are way too long now having about 3 different extension mechanics, every character has lost their gameplay identity, their collaboration works are boring and wasted opportunities to do something actually meaningful or substantial and there are no signs or intentions of making major improvements, given that the last few "fix" patches were, in the grand scheme of things, meaningless and useless.  I've tried every character, gone to offline tournaments, played with friends, and given Tekken 8 a fair chance since release. I'm posting my first review on Steam as a testament to my disappointment with a 30 year old series that has been consistently enjoyable despite some flaws and has taught me so much, yet has fallen so low.  Mr.Harada, please be in charge of Tekken 9, make it a classic, end the Mishima story once and for all and get some rest in Lee's resort in the Bahamas.

Edit after end of season 2:  Having played almost the whole roster and still coming back to casual lobbies daily/weekly it would be hypocritical not to recommend the game. For the "original tekken" experience we still have the old games but for what tekken 8 is it can be a ton of fun with other people in discord. This iteration is the most unforgiving as you have to literally know every interaction if you wan't to know what is going on. Playing basic movement tekken is not a viable strategy anymore and sidestepping/backdashing is mostly for hard reads for very specific situations. Offence is king in this game and "holding block" will just get you killed.  Every patch has been going to the right direction and making it the best it can be with the overly offensive design in mind. I would not recommend this version to casual players who just want to press buttons as it can be very frustrating experience with all the heat stuff and simplified and opressive offensive options that anyone can perform. For fighting game fans, this is still the best 3D fighting game experience (as there is not much competition) that we currently have in the market.   If you want "traditional tekken" with movement options and varied neutral game this is not the game for you, however especially for newcomers this games provides easy access to start playing a fighting game as all characters are loaded with easy to execute moves and strategies. It is a good party game to play in lobby with other people but if you want to play the game competitively you will be faced with a ton of unfair situations where only control you have as a player is to guess from 2 options.   Positive things:  -A lot of characters to choose from -Playing with other people is made a lot easier -Loading times are manageable -Free frame-data in practice with relatively easy options compared to older titles  -Removal of hard legacy inputs for moves that did not need them (universal throw inputs, easier while running input etc.) -Sidestep from ducking was reintroduced (provided, everything tracks so there are rare occasions you actually want to press it)  Negative things:  -This game is 3D in paper but every move tracks making the most viable strategy to spam ob+ tracking moves into pure unearned 50/50 coinflip gameplay -Neutral skip buttons -Magic 4 was removed  -Ki charge counterhit was removed -DLC characters cannot be tested in practice mode -Combos take a ton of time to execute -Mechanics that take you out of playing the game with very long animations (rage arts, heat activations etc.) -Higher health makes poking a lot less viable -Ranked system is still a mixed bag so quality of games is a coinflip  The dev team seems to listen to social media outrage instead of constructed criticism. Players are also promised things that eventually are not what was said like infamous "season 2 defensive patch" where all characters were given more oppressive attacks with low risk high reward type of playstyle. Latest few patches after season 2 farce have been steps to right direction but the road is about 100 steps long so I am not holding my breath on this game actually ever becoming the nuanced competitive game that the earlier installations have been.

This review is written after the v2.03.01 update with the early access release of Fahkumram.  This patch shows the developers have now tripled down on the game's direction, aggression. The skill floor for beginner players has been lowered with heat burst, heat smash, chip damage, unblockables, improved lows, armor moves, homing throws, low risk high reward strings, realigning strings, infinite range weapons, safer/fewer getup options, and rage art. Mechanically difficult options have been made easier or replaced with simpler moves, lowering the skill ceiling for intermediate to advanced players. Professional level players have been affected too but they sit above the ceiling at mastery of the game. They can still be the best, but the removal of depth only removes enjoyment from the game. Everybody can now do the highest damage combo with ease. Combo variety is gone, the best damage and wall carry is accessible to all. Single hit pokes and fast counter hit moves have been being selectively nerfed to encourage the use of big moves. Defensive movement is a non-option with far advancing moves, bigger hit boxes, forced 50/50 sequences, and weaker movement. Too many situations come down to a raw guess. Option selects are almost nonexistent, because characters have been given new coverage moves to their move list from Tekken 7 or added in the season 2 patch. The devs refuse to delete these moves or at least make them terrible. Weakness and character identity has been patched out. Online cheating has gone unanswered, and the best solution was a spreadsheet of Twitter reports. These problem have existed since the launch of Tekken 8 and have not been addressed to a satisfactory extent. The developers have had plenty of time to listen to the community which they pretend to be close to and improve the game, but they would rather appease to the greatest common factor in the hopes of greater player retention.  Bandai Namco has gotten what they wanted. A game for the spectators and casuals. Fast-paced rushdown fights with little neutral or spacing, where your best option is to be the first one swinging. Infinite stages have been removed and tournament rules changed on stage selection to discourage defense and make sure all stages are shown. Matches are now flashy particle effects, lengthy combos with cinematics for flare, and the combo and damage counters to let the audience know that was a big combo. There is a lower time investment to pick up the game and feel like you're good at it by flying up the meaningless online ranks, just enough to get the cash cows into the Tekken Shop to buy the uninspired battle pass and costumes while selling Unreal Engine default shapes and assets from previous games. Bandai Namco has taken the momentum from the success of Tekken 7 and turned it into a game that demands less, provides less, and respects less of the community that made it great.  I know casuals don't want a hard game, but there were better alternatives than to turn Tekken into a party game. Investments should have been made on secondary game modes for casual players. Expand on Arcade Quest, why can I finish a visual novel and a couple bot battles in an afternoon? Why not have modifiers, character leveling, a continued story? Bring in extra features to Tekken ball. Train your ghost. Where is tournament mode? Why is Tekken Force one level in the story? Give character episodes that mean something and advance their story. Add in all the cool cinematics and super moves there. Leave online matches for those that want to make the investment and don't ruin it for those that have already invested.  This game had the legacy and potential to be the best fighting game ever, but now it's a disappointment.  Positives: [list] [*]Roster is good. [*]Graphics are good. [*]Story mode is good. [*]More story expansions like Unforgotten Echoes should be done. [*]Fight lounge and Arcade Quest are great for new players to become familiar with the game. [*]Tekken Ball is fun. [*]Music is good. [*]Jukebox is great. [*]Practice and match queue mode settings and UI display tools are great. [*]My Replay is great, replay takeover is an amazing tool. [*]Customization is good. [/list]

The game is in a very rough state. Here's the good and the bad.  The good:  More fluent gameplay, more responsive controls, new mechanics make the game feel fresh and new, yet still feeling very similar and helping players that have legacy skill with Tekken. Roster is good, characters feel nice, look nice, play nice. Great visuals, great stages, nice new moves, and they add more moves every season. Game was sort of tuned in terms of notations and input to make complex and difficult moves become easier for all, for example some Just Frame moves are not that strict as it used to, and most command grabs got rid of the old "know the button" character specific inputs, and instead all characters now have the uf1+2 input for command grabs. Heat mode is good, and helps in comebacks and cool combos. Makes it look impressive. A bit of a dumbed down version of Tekken compared to older titles.  The bad:  The game *IS* a dumbed down version of Tekken. Lots of moves and new mechanics make the game very imbalanced, and some characters just have better moves that others, and are now easier to perform. Why play my old favourite character (Lee Chaolan) who has very difficult gameplay and difficult inputs and demanding playstyle while I can simply pick another character that does the same, with less effort? It feels unfair and silly. The Tekken Store is a joke, it makes you pay for cosmetics by paying extra money, while you already paid money for it. The Tekken gold coins you get from the game are essentially useless, even more so that it was in Tekken 7. Online play is trash, ranked games have no satisfying rewards when winning, and losing hurts a lot more that winning feels good. Lots of intentional disconnects make the experience worse, cheaters even more. Frequent game disconnects for no reason while it wasnt your fault at all, and yet STILL you get punished by the game, letting you know that if you leave frequent matches, you'll get a penalty. Game is too dumbed down, thus making learning the game mean nothing, since new players and moderate players can spam powerful moves at you (and with the help of Special Mode, which is TOURNAMENT OK), and make winning a match a tedious and tiring process. New season's changes and modifications made the game very awful, and the price tag for the new season pass is basically half the game's FULL PRICE (40€).  Utterly absurd, you can try joining the party and try not taking the game seriously, because I cannot. But you won't have a nice time. Wait for a discount on the game and the season passes, and check again. It's a fun game at some times, but most of the times, I want to break my desk in half. That's all.

But to get the good damage, you had to do harder combos that were harder to execute and had A LOT less leniency. Now, all his combos are easier to some degree to execute. He was considered a skill character along with Kazuya, Lee, and Steve. Now he is washed with the same tools and offensive capabilities that the rest of the cast have that he didn't have before. I have unfortunately decided to take a permanent hiatus from the game until actions are taken to fix the game and overhaul it for a more consistent and not forced interaction game play. As someone who's grown up hearing the sound of fists clashing and electric auras crackling, Tekken 8 feels like coming home—but to a version of that home that's been renovated with passion, fire, and a whole lot of flair.  This isn’t just another sequel—it’s a statement. Tekken 8 takes everything we loved about the series and sharpens it like a well-practiced combo. The graphics? Absolutely gorgeous. Characters move with a weight and fluidity that makes every punch feel satisfying, and every slow-motion finish gives you that adrenaline rush like you're standing right there in the arena. You can feel the hits—especially when you're locked in a last round, toe-to-toe with your rival and the health bars are barely holding on.  The new Heat System? Brilliant. It adds aggression and creativity without overwhelming you. It rewards boldness, which is exactly what a fighting game in 2025 should be about. And speaking of boldness—characters like Kazuya, Jin, and even returning legends like Hwoarang feel fresh again. It’s like the developers understood the soul of Tekken and breathed new life into it.  And the story? Surprisingly deep. Not just another tournament backdrop—this time it’s personal, emotional, and cinematic in a way that makes you want to finish it, not skip it. It feels like the team really cared about telling this chapter right.  But what really makes Tekken 8 stand out… is the heart. The love poured into every detail—from the training modes that genuinely help newcomers, to the intricate move lists veterans can sink their teeth into—shows that this was made not just for players, but by people who live and breathe Tekken.  Tekken 8 is fast, beautiful, and brutally fun. But most of all, it reminds you why you fell in love with fighting games in the first place.  A standing ovation from this lifelong fan. 9.5/10.

so, let me preface this by saying, I’ve been playing the tekken series since essentially Tekken 5.  I was Tekken King, close to Tekken God in Tekken 7.   And I stopped playing this one almost altogether, tone deaf devs made balance changes that made no sense, and while its slowly getting fixed, it should have never went in the direction it did. Giving every character 50/50’s is just insane, especially when those 50/50’s are incredibly easy to start. My character feng, a poking character out of all characters, gets 50/50 mixups from standing, no stance, no play to get to that, just from pressing forward and two kick buttons like what??? Previously the move was just a sidestep check and nothing more, but whoever did the balance patch has clearly never touched feng ONCE in their life, as now its jab punishable, because it does low damage and tracks left??? Whats the logic behind that?  And THATS JUST ONE CHARACTER, don’t even get me started on the others. Like Bryan, Jack-8 in the first few days, it gets worse when you look at it long enough.  My biggest issue with all that, it just took away the value of tekken at its core, the reason i genuinely loved this game series was because every little action you did could affect your victory.  For example, holding back while on the ground let you create distance but you wouldn’t be able to block immediately unless you held up, where you created no distance but you’d be able to block immediately getting up. This very simple intricacy allowed for setups, actual mindgames, real strategy and being able to adapt to your opponent.  And yet they took it out and dumbed to just “hold back and you’ll be safe” Why? Why remove it? So beginners don’t get stomped? There is various ways to help beginners like informing them about that, or perhaps not nerf something so universal. Even techrolling had been dumbed down for almost no reason, something thats been staple in previous tekkens, just gets incredibly dumbed down for no reason? Why remove the complexity, thats what makes tekken so enjoyable, to think before you act out your move. Other fighting games just feel more complex, and not so dumbed down, no unrealistic and unreasonable balance patches.  season one had potential, there was a vision, then Michael Murray comes in, takes away the real technical intricacies of the game, and dumbed it down for basically children. And i ask you again, why?  And you know while i like the idea of tekken’s 8 cosmetic battlepass, there aren’t nearly enough good looking cosmetics to award you for even doing the battlepass, SEASON’S ONES END BP REWARD WAS A BALL WITH A SMILEY FACE ON IT, all that grinding for a smiley face ball on the most niche gamemode of volleyball is insane work.   Listen the TLDR of this, is recently the game has been losing its core values, its logical balance patches, and nonsensical 50/50’s. I just genuinely missed what makes tekken, well, tekken.
